en: Introduction: That which is called "land" (buddhakṣetra) is nothing other than the mind. There is no land apart from the mind, and no mind apart from the land.

This is what Vimalakīrti meant when he said, "When the mind is pure, the land is pure. If one takes the physical mass of flesh to be the mind, or regards the reflected images of objects as the mind, then one has not yet realized [the truth].

If one understands why the mind is called "mind" and why the land of consciousness is called "land," then what is meant by the statement that one should contemplate the Dharma-realm as being entirely mind alone,
and that there is no difference between the three— mind, Buddha, and sentient beings? Yet,
those who mistake the mind for external objects remain in a state of dark ignorance, failing to realize that the tendency toward a single mind has resulted in the division of two lands.
Divergence leads to impurity and purity; from these arise suffering and joy. From suffering and joy arise birth and Buddhahood. All lands are formed by the net of conceptualization.
Since turbid and evil sentient beings cannot even believe this, how could they possibly realize it?

Who, then, would turn their back on defilement and face awakening, giving rise to weariness with the mundane and joy in the supramundane? In this present age, who seeks that which transcends birth and death in a single leap?
The shortcut: the expedient means for liberation from saṃsāra. Apart from this single gate of the Pure Land, where else could it be found?

The Dharma Master Wanlian of the Tiantai school investigated the Chan school deeply and extensively examined the scriptural teachings; yet he did not regard either the Chan school or the doctrinal teachings as the ultimate goal, but took the Pure Land as his final destination.
This too was a thorough realization of the fundamental source, conforming both to the principle and to the capacity of beings.
Therefore, he composed songs and wrote inscriptions, all of which extolled the Pure Land and expressed his thoughts with great eloquence.
The miscellaneous verses in twenty-nine chapters were intended to clarify the nature of the Pure Land, as were the forty-eight titled illustrations.
This is why he extensively extols the Pure Land. His "One Hundred and Eight Verses on Mind-Only" thoroughly investigates the Pure Land;
his "Twenty Verses on the Essentials" encourages the practice of the Pure Land.

Furthermore, there are inscriptions on longing and aversion, and verses of admonition—all of which are repeated and earnest reminders intended for all people to return together to the Pure Land. Indeed, as for Bodhi...
Master Sa’s application of mind was such that benefiting others was even more urgent than benefiting himself.

Fearing that [practitioners] might not know how to cultivate the Pure Land, he compiled these ritual procedures to demonstrate it. Fearing that the Pure Land might be seen as something external to Chan, he further composed the "Ode to the Ox" to harmonize them.
Thus, the Dharma Master had already attained deep faith in the Pure Land and realized it within his own mind.
I have been close friends with the Dharma Master for many years and know his history from beginning to end. At eighteen, he was still carrying firewood;

it was not until twenty that he first shaved his head and donned the robes. While he had not yet reached the stage of formal study, his ability to speak with such tireless eloquence—is this not truly difficult, indeed difficult?
I shall therefore offer a few words at the beginning of this preface to clarify Master Ming’s single-minded devotion to the Pure Land. He never used either doctrine or teaching to engage with others;
this is precisely what is meant by "one who excels in doctrine does not speak of doctrine, and one who excels in teaching does not speak of teaching.
Students of later generations should understand that there is no doctrine that is not teaching, no teaching that is not doctrine, and no Pure Land that is not doctrine and teaching.
It is the earth. I hope you will not bifurcate it into two. This is the preface.
Written by Yuecheng Wu Zhengheng at the Incense-Perfumed Chamber of the San-yi Pavilion, in the first month of spring in the year of Yihai of the Great Qing Guangxu era.
Preface:
The Great Way is as it is, the root of the myriad practices. If this fundamental source were dualistic, to what would my teaching turn?

If the myriad practices are one with True Suchness, how can there be distinctions between delusion and awakening? Since True Suchness possesses the myriad practices, there is thus a discernment of ascent.
Deeply submerged. Human minds differ naturally, yet the Way is fundamentally constant. Before a single thought has arisen, how could there be a thousand paths?
Therefore, when the various sages realize this Way, birth and death are empty and still; when sentient beings are ignorant of this Way, the cycle of rebirth remains vividly present.

Consequently, the Great Awakened One’s compassionate heart could not restrain itself; he manifested birth and established traces, providing the ultimate truth while employing provisional means, proclaiming it through the four types of eloquence.
Discerning the opportune conditions to accord with the Dharma, a single sound is proclaimed in its perfect fullness.

Pointing to both emptiness and existence to benefit sentient beings, although the Buddha’s responses differ, the underlying principle remains ultimately without distinction. Contemplating these myriad manifestations of wondrous function, one sees they are all interconnected within the single nature. To examine this, principle and phenomena are fused as a pair;
the profound meaning is manifest upon the tip of a hair. Yet, between the two thoughts of good and evil, the fruits are summoned amidst ten thousand hardships.
It fills the great void until nothing remains; it saturates the Dharma-realm without exception.

If one realizes that the essence and function of the single mind are mutually identical, one will know that the magnitude of the myriad dharmas is non-arising. In truth, this is returning to the root and source, remaining unchanging while following conditions.

Therefore, as for the multiplicity of immeasurable dharma-gates—whether they extend vertically to the ultimate limit or pervade horizontally across all things—they are contained within the site of awakening of the One Vehicle.

Great! It requires nothing more than intuitive realization of spiritual penetration (*abhijñā*). As the ancients said, "The mind encompasses the great void; its measure pervades the sand-grain worlds"—this is clearly evident.
Now, the ordinary and the sage are of one essence; their resonance and response are without error. They are not obstructed by contraction or expansion, nor do they contend over distance or proximity.

They are not separated by phenomena or principle, nor hindered by coming and going. Thus we know that from east to west, across ten trillion lands, regardless of whether they are superior, middling, or inferior—[all are reached].

Those of inferior faculties can all attain rebirth and behold the Buddha; it is only because the two lands differ in their suffering and bliss, and in their purity and defilement, that one feels attraction toward the former and aversion toward the latter.
This must be regarded with profound earnestness. These are the sincere words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, praised in common by those of the six directions.
If we truly believe, aspire, and hold fast to the Name, there is none who does not personally realize and personally arrive [at that state].

Although their stages may differ in rank, once they reach that place, all are free from birth and death. It can thus be said that throughout the entire lifetime of Śākyamuni’s temporal teachings and the six-character Great Name of Amitābha, no principle is left uncomprised and no capacity is left unreached.
Yet, even those of the highest sanctity in a single lifetime still remain deluded regarding the "screened" [obstacles].
The light of [the Buddha]. As for the common folk of the five turbidities, how could they fathom the fundamental source?

Yet, unable to bear the abandonment of the Bequeathed Teaching, I have thus laid bare my humble sentiments, briefly unfolding a few words to express my shallow views. Thus, as the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said:

"From those who have not yet attained the stages (bhūmi) and below, all are called people of false views. This is precisely what that means. Were it not for the expedient means of the Tathāgata, how could...
This is the profound gateway to the treasure-store. Alas, how can it be that the capacities of sentient beings differ according to whether they are sharp or dull?
Thus, while the Tathāgata’s Dharma remains both difficult and easy, one cannot resolve doubts without relying on verbal instruction, nor can faith be aroused without citing scriptural proof.
I have herein set forth the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to provide equal realization of the partial and the perfect for oneself and others. May all beings within the *dharmadhātu*...
Birth is the retribution of the nine grades of mind-only. Through the sudden realization of the three emptinesses, one personally beholds Amitābha of the ten kalpas;
the infinite transformation bodies together perfect the fruits of the two adornments. While the kalpas of dust may come to an end, the vows of the mind are inexhaustible—thus it is said.
On an auspicious day in the first month of spring in the year of Yihai, the first year of the Guangxu era of the Great Qing,
the Śramaṇī Wanshan Xiaorou of Dong’ou composed this preface at the Yuexi Jingshe.

What is the fundamental intention behind the Buddha’s arising in the Pure Land? It is to uproot the suffering of beings and bestow upon them happiness.

Although it is said that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal, this is nothing other than an exhortation for people to abandon their deviance and return to the correct path. Generally speaking, this encompasses immeasurable teachings.

This applies to every gate; it is so for all gates. If one discusses them individually, among them there is specifically opened a "gate of horizontal transcendence" (*ōjō*), which possesses the further virtue of uprooting suffering and bestowing bliss.
It is the most supreme and extraordinary, differing from others.

Therefore, from the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to the end of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, throughout the teachings of the Buddha’s lifetime, there were more than three hundred assemblies. And...
It is for this reason that every sutra, without exception, guides beings toward the ultimate goal of Sukhāvatī.
Subsequently, when the time for the Buddha-dharma arrived, these sublime teachings spread from the West to the East, being transmitted to China.

During the Jin dynasty at Mount Lu, the Dharma Master Huiyuan received the teaching of the *Nianfo Samādhi* (Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha) through his connection with the Venerable Buddhabhadra, together with his younger brother Huichi and the monk Huiyong.
The court’s worthy and noble officials, recluses, and pure-faith followers, including Que Gongze and others numbering one hundred and twenty-three, formed a society at Donglin.
They carved a wooden tablet to record their vow, calling upon each other by name to aspire for rebirth and together transcend to the Land of Bliss.
Later, when Que Gongze arrived to report his rebirth, his fellow vow-makers were at the Baima Monastery in the Eastern Capital during the night, performing rites on his behalf.
On the anniversary of his death, as the sutras were being recited in the forest palace, everything turned the color of gold. A voice was heard from the air, saying: "I am Duke Goutse.
My prayer to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss has now been fulfilled; therefore, I have come to inform you. Having spoken, he vanished.

From this point on, the transmission of the Pure Land teachings spread without ceasing, its fame resounded throughout the world. Thus, the wind of the Lotus Sutra fanned ever more strongly over time; such is the power of sincere resonance.
Miraculous omens appeared in manifold ways. As for those who attained rebirth in the Pure Land of Vimalacitra and other such realms, who can fathom their number?
Were it not for the supreme perfection and suddenness of this Dharma-gate, how could such a thing be possible? It is because this Dharma-gate is sudden.

The body of the Dharma-realm treasury is the great void without exterior; furthermore, because it is perfectly round, regardless of whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull, provided that faith and aspiration are not deficient, one will be reborn [in the Pure Land] simply by invoking the Name.
Thus, the Mañjuśrī-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra states: "Sentient beings may be foolish and dull, unable to understand through contemplation;

yet if they merely cause the sound of recitation to continue uninterruptedly, they will naturally be reborn in the Buddha-land. Even those of the lowest grade of retribution shall ultimately never fall back."
Therefore, rebirth therein is the first step toward the three great kalpas of cultivation and the fundamental stage for attaining the Ten Epithets of a Buddha.
Thus, one should know that many among those reborn there are "one-life-to-Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha) bodhisattvas.
One should accordingly choose and adopt [rebirth] with single-minded devotion to both lands.

I have heard that when human beings experience suffering and pain, it is because they have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness regarding phenomena and persons; this is true for all who harbor fear.

When one investigates the origin of these conditions, they are all found to stem from the beginningless past: the True Nature fails to maintain its own essence, pursuing instead the realm of delusion because it does not return to the single Reality.
One who clarifies this principle realizes that external objects and the internal mind are fundamentally non-dual. Therefore, [the Great...]

The awakened sages regard others as themselves; they give rise to loving-kindness and exercise compassion, providing protection for a long time. Sentient beings, however, are ignorant of this principle;
instead, they take their own minds to be external objects, thereby splitting them into two separate fragments. Consequently, they delude the mind into creating objective realms.
The mind arises because of objects; one creates karma without ceasing. As the ancient masters said: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created does not perish.
When causes and conditions meet, the retribution must be experienced by oneself. Alas! One creates it and experiences it oneself; what business is it of others?
Thereupon, a sense of weary detachment arises, and one desires to seek liberation. Even if one attains a great awakening like that of Wu Da, [it remains so].

When the time for the retribution of karma arrives, although one may realize through principle that suffering is illusory, in terms of actual fact, its painful manifestations are ultimately difficult to escape.
Since it is thus difficult to endure, you should know that the same applies here.

Therefore, while those who have attained enlightenment may be at ease, how can we, in our present state, dare to engage in lofty talk and broad discourse, claiming that birth-and-death is itself nirvana? (Fine.)

Examine this closely; it is truly cause for great dread. Fortunately, there is the Tathāgata’s ungrudging compassion, which, in the form of the "Unasked Self-Expounded" teaching, reveals the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
It says: "If there are those who hear this, they should make a vow to be born in that land.

Furthermore, it asks: "For what reason is that land called 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī)? Because the sentient beings of that country have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is so named."
Extremely joyful. Observing it from this perspective, the suffering and joy of both self and others can be fully perceived.
Indeed, although [all arises] from the single mind, one cannot fail to exercise selection and rejection; one must inevitably abandon suffering and embrace joy.
The *Easy and Inconceivable Contemplation Sutra* states:
"This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. This is because we ordinary beings possess only the mind that *is* the Buddha but have not yet realized it as such;
therefore, we are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). The Tathāgata has been able to realize that the mind *is* the Buddha and has already accomplished it; therefore, he is named Amitābha. Thus...

Through Amitābha, that which is non-attained is realized; this is entirely the realization of what sentient beings possess. That which sentient beings possess is non-existent as a possession; this is entirely the possession of what Amitābha realizes.
Therefore, when a person recollects the Buddha, they are themselves the Buddha. It is like a minister transmitting an imperial decree—he is himself the King.
Although the names of the sentient being’s mind and the Buddha differ, their inconceivable essence is one. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: Mañjuśrī...
He questioned the Buddha: "How may one quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? The Buddha replied: "There is a samādhi called the 'One Practice Samādhi.
One who wishes to enter this One Practice Samādhi should do so in a secluded place, abandoning all distracted thoughts and not grasping at external appearances.

One should fix the mind on a single Buddha, single-mindedly reciting that Buddha’s name. Facing the direction where that Buddha resides, with body upright and directed forward, one should, regarding that single Buddha, maintain mindfulness in every thought-moment."
This continuity is precisely within this very thought. One is able to see all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;

day and night they constantly preach, and their wisdom and eloquence never cease. Contemplating this, who would dare to disparage the recollection of the Buddha? Such [a disparaging attitude] is the act of foolish men and women. Why is this?
It is because within this very thought, one is immediately able to see all that exists throughout the three periods of time.
O Treasure, even all the lands that constitute the environment and its support are contained within this; what further thing could exist outside of the mind?
As for the question and answer, "That which is attained swiftly" is precisely it—these four characters directly point to *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation). This is the first public case (*gong'an*).
Therefore, throughout the ten ages of past and present, the beginning and end do not depart from the present moment of thought; the boundless oceans of lands, self and other...
There is not even a hair’s breadth of separation; this refers precisely to the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).
How inconceivable it is! Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The divine eye of the *śrāvaka* is but the fleshly eye; for one who studies the Mahāyāna, the fleshly eye becomes the Buddha-eye.

Therefore, practicing the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is like a person on a boat in the great ocean: when looking in all four directions, everything is uniformly water, and thus there is no need to seek anything else.
This is like digging for a spring on dry land; it simply requires valuing the single mind that seeks birth [in the Pure Land]. Be careful, be careful!

Regarding the non-duality of mind and land, Zhiyi went to consult Master Zhigong, who said: "The wise know that the mind is Buddha; the ignorant delight in going to the West. How can these two be the same?"
The answer is: Do you not know what Master Yongming said? "If the ancient worthies had words of exclusion or limitation, they were all intended for the sake of beings to dispel attachments;
thus, one must not rely solely on their words without relying on their meaning.

This is precisely to refute people's attachment to the view of permanence and their failure to realize the ultimate depth of their own minds, whereby they seek exclusively outwardly. If one realizes this, then [one does not seek] outwardly.
This is the essential purport of the inner [teachings]: the single system is thus tranquil and expansive. Master Zhìgōng certainly did not speak these words; however, he did say:
"The wise know that the mind is Buddha, because the mind has no exterior. This is the natural state (*tianyánzhīrán*); fundamentally, there is no contrived activity.

Thus, the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are contained within it. Therefore, the mind encompasses the vast void and its measure pervades the sands of the world-systems. Even the hells arise therein."
The mind of wondrous enlightenment—how could it be that only the land of Amitābha Buddha in the Western Quarter is not this very mind?
Since the Land of Bliss is precisely my own mind, when I know that land, I know my own mind; when I contemplate that Buddha, I contemplate my own mind.
The land is the land of one’s own mind, and the mind is the mind of one’s own land. Mind and land are non-dual; sentient beings and Buddhas are one.
It is settled; there is not even a hair’s breadth of error. If this is so, what folly could there be in reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth?
The *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* records Mañjuśrī recounting his own past causes, stating that he attained the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* and shall be born in the Pure Land.
The World-Honored One further prophesied to him: "You shall be reborn in the world of Ultimate Bliss. Thus, the verse from the *Mañjuśrī-praṇidhāna-sūtra* says:
He said: "May I, at the time of my life's end, be completely cleared of all obstacles, behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face, and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Having been born in that Buddha-land, may I fulfill my great vows; may Amitābha Tathāgata appear before me and bestow upon me the prophecy of enlightenment.
Now, if even Mañjuśrī—the greatest among those of great wisdom within the Mahāyāna—yet went along with them, then how much more so [should] Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna?
That this celestial robe contains the Perfect Illumination of the Original [Nature] and so forth goes without saying.

Why, then, would one who knows that the mind is Buddha not seek rebirth? If even the wise, knowing the mind is Buddha, still seek rebirth, then it stands to reason that the ignorant seeking rebirth is but natural.
Regarding the identity and difference of the Mind-only, Mencius said:
"Words that are near yet point to what is far-reaching are excellent words; principles that are concise yet yield broad application are excellent paths.

How much more so is this regarding the Way of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world—a Way which, the more one looks up to it, the higher it seems; the more one drills into it, the more solid it proves. All sentient beings...
That which ordinary beings cannot fathom is the essence of the Great Way mind; it is realized solely by the Buddhas. It is perfectly luminous and penetrating, entirely free from obstruction.
Therefore, the three types of wisdom are known within a single moment of mind, and the five eyes are seen within a single eye.

All the pure lands of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time are inherently possessed within one's own mind; hence, the word "solely" (*wei*) is used. *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* (Verse):

It is said: "The four great continents, the sun and moon, the Sumeru mountains, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds—each of these one thousand constitutes what is called a 'small chiliocosm.

A thousand times this small chiliocosm is termed a 'medium chiliocosm. A thousand times this medium chiliocosm is a 'great trichiliocosm,' all of which share the same period of formation and destruction.
One such great trichiliocosm is called a single Buddha-field (buddhakṣetra), consisting of ten billion suns and moons and ten billion Sumeru mountains."
A hundred billion sets of the four great oceans and a hundred billion Iron Ring Mountains constitute the vast extent of a single Buddha-field.
By this analogy, one can see that all the Buddha-fields of the Buddhas are likewise. To the west from here, passing through a hundred trillion Buddha-fields, lies the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Viewed in this way, that land is extremely distant from here; yet it stands majestic with jeweled trees, jeweled ponds, and railings.
The railings, the nets, the four-colored lotuses, and the assembly of holy ones gathered in the ocean-like congregation—these are not matters of analogy, inference, or conventional dharma;
they are actual phenomena. They are not other things, nor do they come from without;
they are all the vastness of my own mind, and thus it encompasses such Buddha-lands. Yet this is not unique to me alone; therefore, the lands of all Buddhas are likewise [only my mind].
It is also acceptable to include the ant’s mind. Why? Because although the ant’s body is minute, its mind is likewise vast.
If one realizes this, there will be no doubt and no obstruction whatsoever; only then can it be called the "Pure Land of Mind-Only.
If it were otherwise, then all Buddha-lands would exist outside the mind. Though such a claim might sound the same when spoken with the mouth, when it comes to seeing [the truth],...
The mind, however, is different; it cannot be termed "mind-only" [in the same sense]. Generally speaking, when discussing their commonality, the mind encompasses the vast void (*mahāśūnyatā*).

This is as seen in masters such as Yongming Yanshou and Chushi Zhiyuan of Mount Lu, who, upon seeing the Buddha, sought rebirth in the Western Land, asserting that "mind-only" was the underlying principle.
When discussing their differences, the vast void encompasses the mind; thus they say that the Pure Land is right before one's eyes, and Amitābha is not in the West.
As for "the square," it is simply that his mind is different from others. Why, then, would he play the lute at my gate? What does this saying of Confucius mean? Therefore, Xuansha said:
"Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real; it is only because they have long been identifying with the conscious spirit.
This has been the root of birth and death for immeasurable kalpas, yet deluded people call it the 'Original Person. (The Śūraṅgama Sūtra)

It is said: "Those who have fallen into the path of demons take what is directly before them to be the Buddha-land, claiming there is no separate Pure Abode, nor any golden marks and signs of excellence.
If one contemplates the words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as if looking into a bright mirror, then the beautiful and the ugly will be clearly visible.

Question: When one contemplates the identity of the mind and the Buddha, observing that there is nothing external, since the mind is fundamentally without form, how can it have a location? Answer: If it has no location, how could I speak to you of it?

Question: What, then, is the mind? Answer: It is the six great characters [of the Name]. Question: If this is so, is it not the case that one is recollecting the mind rather than recollecting the Buddha? Answer: [As follows...]
"The mind and the Buddha are one and the same. He asked Zhaozhou, "When one recites the Buddha's name once, it rinses the mouth for three days.
How can they be one and the same? Zhaozhou replied, "In general, the Patriarchs' way of engaging with beings is not fixed;
sometimes it is so, and sometimes it is not. The *Mizang Zhinan* (Guide to the Secret Treasury) states: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the Dharma-body of Vairocana? Zhaozhou said, "Amitābha."
"Amitābha Buddha! Amitābha Buddha!"—since these are His sincere words, how could Zhaozhou have ever failed to recite the Buddha's name?
Therefore, for those of wondrous realization, principle and phenomena operate in tandem; they are like the two wings of a bird or the two wheels of a chariot, neither of which can be lacking.
You know only this, but have never known that. Sit down and rinse your mouth;

upon seeing it once, you should understand that at the very moment of recollecting the Buddha, one must investigate the mind that is capable of recollecting. That which pervades all places is utterly unobtainable.

This is called "recollection without recollection," which is the contemplation of the mind through the contemplation of emptiness while recollecting the Buddha. Take this very mind that is capable of recollecting and recollect...
The name of the Buddha he contemplates becomes distinct and vividly clear; this is called "contemplating through non-contemplation.
This refers to using provisional contemplation (*parikalpita-ālambana*) to observe the mind that contemplates the Buddha.

In this way, in every thought-moment, one thoroughly realizes that the contemplating mind and the contemplated Buddha are neither empty nor existent; both extremes are unattainable. It is neither self nor other—the Middle Way.
It is also non-existent. It is quiescent yet illuminating; one contemplates within one's own mind and becomes a Buddha. It is illuminating yet quiescent; that Buddha manifests one's own mind.

that those who attain rebirth there do not do so [to return]. Alas! You have misunderstood the intent of the Buddhist scriptures. You should know that this is the meaning of the Sanskrit term.

Because after that stage of the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one acts spontaneously through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). When entering the Sahā world, one does not lose [this state].

Mind. This refers to those of the lowest-of-the-low grade; even when such people of the ten evil deeds reach that land, they still give rise to the bodhicitta.

If even the Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna are thus, how could I dare to harbor self-conceit?

Therefore, when a person is about to give rise to a thought, if they do not even examine themselves to see whether this thought is good or evil, can they not be said to lack vigilance?
Now, each of you should test yourselves: from morning until evening, and from evening until dawn, there is certainly no moment when thoughts do not arise.
If such thoughts arise, it is certain that one will subsequently receive a body; once a body is received...

The body certainly does not fail to receive retribution; once retribution is received, it certainly does not fail to be either suffering or pleasure. If one distinguishes between suffering and pleasure, one certainly cannot avoid accepting or rejecting them.
If the mind of acceptance and rejection arises, one certainly cannot refrain from practicing and maintaining [the path]. If one knows the swift essentials of practice and maintenance...

There is absolutely no one who does not believe in the Buddha. Why is this? It is because the Buddha arises from mindfulness. If one does not give rise to the thought of the Buddha, then one gives rise to distracted thoughts.
Thus, the two fruits of suffering and happiness have their cause in the thoughts arising right now. Therefore, the *Samādhi Sūtra* says: "A single thought receives a single body;
a wholesome thought results in a body among gods or humans, while an unwholesome thought results in a body in the three evil realms. (100)

the bones, marrow, skin, and hair will fill the lands of the great trichiliocosm such that there is no empty space remaining. If not even a single thought arises, one is tranquil.
Return to the source. Now, these sutras are the words of the Buddha; how could one not believe them? Alas!

"Why do you emit light to frighten me? Turn it back quickly and recite the name again! The ghost said in fear, "In a single thought-moment, a five-colored light of over ten zhang suddenly radiates from your chest, dazzling my eyes and mind.

How could there be any doubt about this? Indeed, light can dispel darkness; even if there were a dark place where one might be deluded..."
When one brings this to mind, it is extinguished immediately through the majestic radiance of the Buddha. This is illustrated by the analogy of a blind person in the daytime:

even if they have the delusive perception of seeing darkness, that perception is extinguished on the spot upon encountering the brilliant light of the sun. Therefore, the eighth fascicle of the Venerable Master Zhìzhì’s *Ten Doubts* says:

It is like a dark room ten thousand years old: when the sunlight briefly reaches it, the darkness is instantly extinguished. How could it be that the long-standing darkness refuses to be extinguished?

It is also like being struck by a poisoned arrow; though the shaft is deep and the venom is cruel, wounding the flesh and breaking the bone, as soon as one hears of the medicinal drum that eliminates it, the arrow is extracted and the poison removed.

Furthermore, his original vow states: "When the bodhisattvas from other buddha-lands come to be born in my land, they shall ultimately and inevitably reach the stage of being 'one birth away from Buddhahood' (ekajātipratibaddha).

This mindfulness of the Buddha is like the faith of a person. One should beforehand practice this visualization until it is thoroughly mastered, so that at the moment of death, one's thoughts will surely be directed toward the west.
Regarding the determination of the vow:
the practitioner’s aspiration must be as urgent as that of a Mahānāga, a great and powerful hero, whose forehead necessarily breaks out in a boil when he is enraged;
so long as that boil has not yet healed, there is no person in Jambudvīpa who can oppose him.
It is so. For this person who practices *nien-fo*, their vow is likewise: through a single act of faith in rebirth, they may escape this cycle of *saṃsāra*.
One must certainly establish a vow; as long as that vow is not yet fulfilled, the circumstances of compliance and resistance within Jambudvīpa shall not obstruct you.
Regarding "establishing practice with firm vigor":
this refers to a practitioner who must gain mastery over their own conduct. It is like the debate between Bhāviveka and a non-Buddhist follower of the *asaṃjñika* school.

Because their power is firm and fierce, there will also be words of response on the following day. Since there are words of response, it is because they have entrusted their substance to a stubborn stone.

So that it may circulate in the future, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma-seat and manifested great supernormal powers.

Thus, what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected should be understood accordingly. However, in general, the Buddha’s intent does not exceed this:

Such a person shall not fall into the evil realms. Eleventh, in future lives they will be able to revere and honor the Triple Gem, attain rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Life, become a great Bodhisattva, and eventually achieve Buddhahood and enter the path of Nirvana. It is further said:

if a person, at the time of death, speaks of creating an image even as small as a grain of wheat, they can eliminate the cycle of birth and death for eighty billion kalpas across the three periods of time.

Regarding this sin: according to this, if merely speaking at the moment of death to commission the creation of an image results in inconceivable merit, how much more so when one now personally pierces one’s own tongue?
If creating an image with silver coins results in inconceivable merit, how much more so when one now offers this single piece of blood-cleansed sincerity?
Thus, in seeking rebirth in the Western Paradise, one must establish pure conditions with that Buddha; this is most [essential].
There is nothing more kind than this. Because of it, I have come to admire and revere these matters.
Beginning in the year of Xinwei and ending in Guiyou, I have painted over three hundred and sixty scrolls of sacred images.
Among them, I have composed forty-eight verses as I painted, recording my thoughts to serve as a means for establishing karmic connections with the Pure Land for all faithful men and women.
Truly rejoicing in the arousal of the bodhicitta, those who wish to prick their blood and carefully copy [this text] must first burn incense and, facing west, make this vow:

"May we quickly escape the sea of suffering and suddenly transcend to the Land of Bliss. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one performs meritorious deeds without making a vow, nothing will be established."
May you become a guide, capable of achieving [this goal]. It is like melting gold: it follows whatever the master fashions, for the gold has no fixed form.
Now, piercing the blood to create a Buddha is likewise; when the vow for the Pure Land is established, one will naturally attain it later.

Whether wise or foolish, all alike shall shatter the solid mountain of the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). This attachment, though seemingly unbreakable, shall be severed by itself—be they monastics or laypeople.
Together we shall uproot the very source of birth and death. In that Pure Land, non-arising arises of itself;
may I leave behind the land of the five turbidities and personally taste the nectar of immortality. When the thorns on my tongue are no longer so many, in which rank shall my merit be inscribed?
The whole heart is the Buddha of Blood; his entire body radiates beams of light. The dream of the Western Arrival is shattered; the icy soul is pure with auspicious fragrance.
He pricked his own blood solely for the sake of the cause of liberation from suffering; he burned incense and entrusted his brush to transmit the divine with wondrous skill.
May the Compassionate Father grant me his acceptance, so that I may soon become one among the people of the Land of Coolness.
Behold me sinking and drowning; the Great Sage pities me. In response to my capacity, he manifests and enters into this painting.

After the blood coagulated at the tip of his tongue, forming a karmic bond with the Buddha, We shall follow one another through eternal kalpas, our lot never to be parted. (These three verses above are written in the rhyme of Chan Master Chewu.)
People are themselves Vairocana, yet they remain deluded; the Tathāgata has sent me to point the way back to the West. With the blood of one's heart, one transcribes the Buddha of the Mind;
upon the four-colored lotus, the nine grades are inscribed.
The numinous nature originally possessed by both sentient beings and Buddhas is like the brilliant color of blood-flowers, surpassing even the finest pigments.
Though it is the same as the white ox on the open ground, only when it passes through the window lattice to the west does the Way finally find rest.

When the Buddha practiced austerities for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he was my child who turned his back on awakening and joined with the dust of the senses. Though my body may be ground to powder and shattered to pieces, his kindness is difficult to repay;
thus, I shall depict his form and likeness with my own blood.
Long detained in this Sahā world, I have endured every affliction; taking up my blade to cut through the flesh and blood, how could I fear the hardship?
With sincere heart, I make this vow to return to the West, so that I may soon cast off the ailments of birth, old age, and death in this floating life.
May the Lotus Buddha-land open wide its gates; may not a single sentient being be cast aside as waste. My heart is indeed filled with nothing but fervent blood;
morning after morning, I gaze toward it, longing to sing the song of my return.

In wishing to form a karmic bond with the fragrance, whom do I seek as my kin? I respectfully use my own blood to paint the Buddha’s spirit. At the Lotus Pond assembly, may you forgive my late return;
pure mindfulness is difficult to maintain consistently, while habitual tendencies easily renew themselves.
Now my study has been sealed by indolence; I have painted extra images of kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. I give this blood-written letter as a covenant to all people:
may we meet again one day at the Lotus Pond.

The hope for blessings lies between heaven and humanity; yet with the power of forbearance not yet formidable, all remains stubborn. Cut open your heart’s blood and diligently recite the Buddha’s name;
wait until you have attained rebirth before you can deliver sentient beings.
Blood is the very mind that forms the Buddha-body; through the realization of the non-differentiation of the three, one awakens to the prior cause.
All you great ones, enter the Lotus Treasury and together receive the prediction of enlightenment from Amitābha.

Wiping away blood and lightening the body, pure mindfulness arises; herein, one does not borrow even the slightest lightness. When the child returns to the father’s place, what object is there to rely upon?
This Way is difficult to accomplish, while that is easy to accomplish.
Kuizi gazes toward the shore of the other realm where you dwell; though blood-stained images of the Sage resemble one another, none can truly match them.
I pray that you will fill the ocean of sorrow within that heart, and raise me from my sinking with your own hands.
Unchanging while following conditions, it envelops empty space; unchanging yet following conditions, it resides within the span of a single cubit. Reveal this upon my hands of *tūla* cotton:
its subtle resonance is like a flower, brilliant and a vivid crimson.
Sincere devotion moves the Buddha to arrive at Donghua; his hands hang down clearly, forming a slanting mudrā. Do not say that being without mind implies having no form;
the flower wheels beneath his feet are as large as chariots.
The crimson flesh-protuberance of the Buddha is encircled by a halo; the flower petals are more vividly fresh with subtle, pale markings.
Upon seeing the true emptiness, one attains the highest rank of the heart—where else could one possibly penetrate the three barriers?
Lineage upon lineage, kinship and blood are truly real; it is as if those who have been reborn as Flower-Buddhas. Now I ask you all:
is it his body, or is it your own?
The body of our Buddha is not pierced by blood; its original nature gives rise to its countenance spontaneously.
Those who attempt to deliberate or calculate within this have not yet reached Yunmen’s Single-Word Barrier.
Dropping the blood, one should cause it to reach the fundamental reality. We share the same essence as the Buddha’s spirit;
when True Suchness is not yet realized, the person differs from the Buddha, but once True Suchness is realized, even the Buddha is but a person.
The *svastika* of the Sanskrit script is written in blood upon his chest; pure and inherently so, it is unstained by dust.
Coming from nowhere and going nowhere, he is thus named the Ancient Tathāgata.
Tongue-blood flowers bloom amidst the lunar halo; their pale red brilliance reflects between the green waves.

Had the Five Masters not skillfully transmitted this manual, how could we recognize the Sage’s countenance today? (The Five Masters refers to the five mentioned below who possess supernatural powers.)
Buddha-bodies fill all realms as numerous as motes of dust; though people do not see them, their aggregates remain unemptied.
Fortunate that Great Compassion takes pity on me, you have rolled yourself forth to appear within this fragment of my sincere devotion.
I fix my direction toward the West; there is no need to seek the Buddha in the meditation hall.
I only hope that when the spirit departs, I may return home and share a single niche with Amitābha.
The vow for rebirth in the Pure Land stands as heavy as a mountain; when the Dharma-realm is fully illuminated, I too shall return. With my tongue split, I truly offer blood beneath the blade;
let this heart be fashioned into a jade platter and distributed.
Blood replaces the various lords, revealing their original countenance; the spiral topknots and Buddha-locks are a pale, rosy hue. May we, meeting in our hearts, arrive together upon the lotus pond;
the flowers bloom of themselves, and the waters flow of themselves. (Written in the autumn of the Xinwei year, following the original rhyme of the San-yi Jushi.)
The blood-stained points are the numinous light of the Buddha-nature unfolding; the red-painted petals are artfully arranged as if planted.

Who knows who possessed the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) to behold the golden countenance directly upon the tree? (The "Five Powers" refers to the monk from the Kukkutapāda Monastery in India who traveled to the West to seek the likeness of the Buddha. Upon his return, the Buddha had already appeared upon the leaves of a tree;
he thus used pigments and brushes to transcribe it, hence this [image] exists.)
Who is it whose blood paints these blossoming flowers? Do not say they have never been planted upon the water.
Though the myriad purples and thousands of reds differ in their forms, they all return to the root from within this very place.
With the sword of wisdom, he carved his flesh to repay the kindness of his teacher; he severed all distinctions and manifold attachments.
Walking with simple faith, he returned to his native village, only then realizing that the golden arm was none other than the mind itself hanging down.
From beginning to end, disciple follows disciple and teacher follows teacher; neither identical to Amitābha nor separate from him. Blood becomes countless Buddhas as emanations;
throughout the ten directions they appear, their hands reaching down in unison.
Blood soaks the crimson blossoms, drenched by tears and sobs; following the two streams, I seek out the blessings from the West. A single path leads straight to the Way of the Source;
how could the golden mouth’s direct transmission ever be a false sound?
Returning to my native land, my tears flow in torrents; across the star-studded canvas, I seek traces of blood.
Apart from the kingdom of Sūmātra, where else can I find a true companion?
Whose blood was used to paint this Buddha? This person has manifested as a Buddha with great clarity.
Such a portion of the Tathāgata’s true suchness (tathatā) must surely be the mind of Lake-Heart (Hradacitta) who attained rebirth there.
With the blood from his tongue-tip, he paints the Buddha’s body; its reflection in the flower pond illuminates the depths. Raising his foot, he overturns the path of coming and going;
his spirit returns to the watery realm to speak of non-arising.
In silent contemplation before the fragrant offering, I carve away a portion of my own body; blood stains the jade fan, its wondrous truth most extraordinary.
Human life is like a lump of charcoal in a red furnace, casting out the mold of emptiness beyond the world.

The golden blade emerges from its scabbard, cleaving the floating carcass; it raises up the lotus flower, its green canopy most extraordinary. From this point on, one should return to personally behold the Buddha;
untying the brow, one gazes at the pattern within the matured blood.

The wondrous, luminous essence of awakening is fundamentally at peace; without moving so much as a hair’s breadth, it is revealed upon the tip of the tongue. My compassionate mother weeps with blood, surely mindful of me;
I gaze from the railing, bathing in the waters of autumn.
Master and disciple are in perfect accord, both at ease; together they abide in the non-dual state of the perfect pearl. The blood from his tongue fully reveals the wondrous and subtle essence;
thus, whether ordinary or sage, one may behold it directly.
Faithfully I turn toward the ancient Buddhas of the Western Land; their vermilion-golden countenances rest upon pedestals of blood-red lotuses.
They manifest their bodies in the posture for subduing Māra, and the sound of their footsteps is like the thundering of the earth’s foundations.

The Amitābha written in blood is from the very beginning; taking birth, one returns to borrow the Terrace of the Water Goddess. With the sincerity of a chrysanthemum, I cast myself to the ground and offer incense in supplication;
my body is like a collapsing mountain, and my cry is like thunder.
On the first day, the lotus blooms and the Buddha awakens; with a compassionate heart, he manifests the numinous power of precious light. Returning, he calls me to go back to the West;
the mountains are green and the waters are green.
The image of fresh blood is tranquil yet alert; where both alertness and tranquility are forgotten, it becomes even more vital. The four-colored lotus flowers do not age in spring;
the round leaves fill the pond, all a lush green.
With sincere devotion, paint the ever-renewing crimson; directly upon this ordinary body, manifest the Buddha-body. Amidst the brief interval of dreams, who is the master?
Without departing from pure tranquility, one rescues the red dust of the mundane world.
The tip of my tongue pierces through blood, fresh and new; it paints the red banner as an offering to the Buddha’s body. By nature we are kin, true father and son;
life after life you have led me away from the dust and mire.
Encompassing the vast void, all returns to the single truth; within this, there is nothing that is not revered and cherished. Who knows whose blood flows from the ultimate source?
It is painted as the body of Vairocana beneath the emerald canopy.
The true Buddha is within the very blood and heart; holy and ordinary beings share the same essence, fundamentally kin.
Everyone, rouse your spirits and look: all are bodies of untrammeled freedom.
In the pond of eight virtues, the jade well has blossomed; he took the blood from his tongue to serve as the root and seed.
Such sincerity is truly inconceivable; it moved our Buddha of the West to come.
Blood-stained lotuses draw forth emerald blooms; all are planted by having shed this illusory body. To deliver sentient beings, one must realize the patience of non-arising;
follow the Buddha to be reborn in his land—come and go!
"Mind itself is Buddha" (from the *Fisherman*) also includes the account of Mazu’s single transmission;
it likewise points to the Jewel King Samādhi. Therefore, it is said that "mind itself is Buddha.
To say "mind itself is Buddha" means that reality is present within phenomena; it clarifies that the practice of nianfo (buddha-recitation) is the very foundation of attaining Buddhahood.
This is because his intention was precisely to cause every person to initiate cultivation from this point. Furthermore, he said, "Neither mind, nor Buddha.

This was intended for those who have misconceptions regarding the mind and falsely identify with it; he sought to protect them from errors and prevent such delusions. However, this is not yet the direct realization of the knowledge and vision of the Buddha-mind within oneself.
To examine the knowledge and vision of the Buddha in detail, as the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "To see the reality of all dharmas..."

To perceive these marks is called "seeing the Buddha. Now, if all phenomena are thus, and it is certain that there has never been a Teacher for ten kalpas whose great name of myriad virtues is not the Buddha, then by this one knows that "mind is itself Buddha.
This fully accords with those of superior capacity. As for "neither mind nor Buddha," [it accords with those of middling capacity].
This is merely said because the capacities [of the listeners] are not favorable. If one discusses the great purport, it cannot even be characterized as "one.
This is precisely the statement that "it is not two"; therefore, it is a provisional designation. Ultimately, the supreme principle returns to the same source: it is neither deep nor shallow.

It is not identity, nor is it difference. However, because later generations who study the Way fail to comprehend this, they conversely claim that reciting the Buddha’s name and cultivating the mind has not yet reached the profound and mysterious.
They place exclusive emphasis on the obliteration of all traces and non-reliance as the ultimate principle. How lamentable this is!
Throughout the ten ages of past and present, it never changes or shifts. At every moment, before one’s parents were born, it is wondrously maintained and uniquely so; it is spontaneously thus.
Beyond the six characters of the Great Name, there is no Chan.
The Buddha is identical to the mind, encompassing the vast void; it pervades the entire realm of sands without exception. Sounds are distinct and clear; the mind is as it truly is.
One arrives riding the white ox-cart on the open ground.
Attaining what is called the profound and wondrous Chan, one pierces through seventeen hundred knots; the cause becomes ever more concise, and the fruit becomes ever more perfect.
Too lazy to open my mouth further to discuss the ultimate source.

In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where ordinary beings and sages dwell together—who would have known that its reality penetrates both the partial and the perfect? Offering flowers to the Buddhas, one rides upon lotuses;
coming and going throughout the ten directions, the essence remains serene.
The Four Great Vows (in *Yujia’ao*) and the Preface to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* state:
"If one does not give rise to the great vows, one will be possessed by Māra. Indeed, the vow is the mind itself.

There is no vow apart from the mind, and no mind apart from the vow. Therefore, for those who have attained awakening, because the mind is vast, their vows are likewise vast. For those who are deluded...
Because their minds are small, their aspirations are also small. Therefore, one uses the Four Great Vows to broaden the mind.
If one can realize that one's own mind is vast and that nothing exists outside of it, then the Great Vows will be established from this point forward.
Since the causes of these Four Great Vows all arise solely from one's own mind, the fruits of the Four Great Vows likewise arise solely from one's own mind.
It is full. That being so, it is not enough to be ignorant of the Dharma-gates for delivering sentient beings.
Since both sentient beings and afflictions are immeasurable, the Dharma-gates I study must likewise be immeasurable. Therefore, the Four Great Vows are the very source of entering the Way.
For this reason, it is further said: "One need not concern oneself with a trichiliocosm filled to capacity..."
Precious jewels! I pray that you will joyfully listen. Because there was not even a single phrase of the Buddha-dharma yet heard, Sudhana traveled south in search of it;
such was his practice of an earnest mind for the sake of the Dharma. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"If one can give rise to a single thought, saying, 'May I become a Buddha and extinguish the suffering of all sentient beings,' then even though one has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) nor performed difficult deeds, by virtue of this mind..."
Because its mouth is heavy, it surpasses all sentient beings; this is because its vows during the stage of the causal ground are great, and thus it surpasses all.

The *Huanyuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source) says: "When truth encompasses the root of delusion, there is no practice that is not cultivated; when delusion penetrates the source of truth, there is no characteristic that is not quiescent."
For this reason, the great Bodhisattvas practice throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* without perceiving any sign of birth; it is precisely because of this.
As for us ordinary people, since our power of patience (*kṣānti*) is not yet sufficient, we can only wait until they have been born in the Pure Land.
Only then may you swiftly enter and return here to perform great Buddha-work.

I pray that you deliver all sentient beings of the six realms from their states of suffering. The cycles of sorrow, joy, separation, and union increase my fear; I earnestly exhort the people of the world to keep [these] far away.
Reflect! You must awaken. Honor, splendor, wealth, and nobility are like frost and dew; you should know that this burning house cannot be inhabited for long.

With single-minded devotion, recite the Buddha’s name and depart for the Western Land. When you behold Amitābha face-to-face, he will turn his head and look back upon you. It is not yet too late; at that time, you shall deliver all those who have been your enemies and kin throughout kalpas of past lives.
I pray that you sever the blazing afflictions that scorch my eaves. The path to Nirvana stands blocked before me. A hundred thousand obstructing māras emerge together from their dwellings;
their majesty is like tigers, baring their sharp fangs and claws to harm the Master. Where can one hide the body to escape this suffering? One.
With a mind mindful of the Buddha, I seek my compassionate father. At birth, may there be no birth, as I am born into the Pure Land. In the end, this shall not be in vain;
may we all together become companions among the lotus flowers.
I vow to study [this].
I vow to study all immeasurable Dharma-gates together. May the Tathāgata extinguish all my evils for me. My practice shall not conflict with others, and I shall never err.
Awakening from the alarm of dhyāna, the practitioner avoids sitting in the delusion of empty space. The Pure Land is mind-only; depart from the five turbidities.

With single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one transcends horizontally and swiftly. The dream of Nanke is shattered, and like a cicada, one sheds its shell. In the Vairocana pavilion, there is carefree joy.
Riding upon the lotus calyx, may you vow to attain the Buddha-way and perfect the unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. Your originally pure mind is transcendent; through three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—
Practice together with fellow students. It is like a jade image being completed through carving; the blade of wisdom sweeps away millions of fetters.

Single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name is no bondage; it universally transforms all sentient beings to return to perfect enlightenment. True, eternal bliss—nirvana and birth-and-death are like flowers falling from the sky.
Regarding the four immeasurable minds (the preceding preparatory stage), the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"Because he is endowed with merit, he does not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because he is endowed with wisdom, he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because of his great compassion, he does not dwell in the unconditioned; because he fulfills his original vows, he does not exhaust the conditioned. Thus it is said.
His appearance in the world is nothing other than for the purpose of uprooting the suffering of sentient beings and bestowing happiness upon them;
he desires to cause all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, so that they may share in what he himself has realized. Furthermore, it is said: "The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body.
It arises from immeasurable merit and wisdom; it arises from kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; it arises from giving."

Through the practice of ethical discipline, patience, gentleness, diligent application of energy, meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, extensive learning, and wisdom—the various pāramitās arise;
even up to the severing of all unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas, the body of the Tathāgata is produced.
Although the Buddha’s intention is thus, it is nonetheless necessary for people to enter with faith and cultivate according to the Dharma.
[If this were not so,] it would be proven otherwise. It would be a vain labor for the Tathāgata to appear in the world; his single teaching would be in vain—what benefit would there be for humanity?

The Great Compassionate Buddhas constantly bestow happiness through their great compassion. One must realize the spiritual method and wondrous medicine, which can cure the afflictions of sentient beings.
Thin as a cloud-curtain, sweet rain falls evenly upon all under heaven. The Way has many divergent paths that are difficult to fathom;
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind can never be wrong. It allows my spirit to dwell within the calyx of a red lotus. Do not harbor doubts;
thus you shall avoid drifting through the sea of suffering.

The Great Compassionate Buddhas constantly uproot suffering through their great compassion. Having reverently heard the遗训 (bequeathed instructions) and the words of the Capable One (Nagarjuna), I bow my head to Amitābha, the Teacher of the World.
Through the convergence of fragrant conditions, I now exhort all men and women: in this degenerate age, one can only cultivate the Pure Land. One.

In my heart, I take the Buddha as my companion; the grace of the Compassionate Father is as deep as the sea. From the blooming lotus, in every atom and every land, I repay the milk of the Master with great joy.

The Buddha rejoices that sentient beings leave the realms of suffering; that sentient beings attain happiness is praised by the Tathāgata. He leads them into the Dharma-light of tranquility to dwell together therein.
Carefree and at ease, all manner of adornments manifest according to their nature. I have already known the essential task: with a single mind, recite the Buddha’s name and transmit it to others.
I only wish that every person would deeply and far-reachingly aspire to this. A torch of radiant light—coral and agate.
The Pearl Tree:

The Great Renunciation of the Buddha, who renounced both enemies and kin with equanimity; having returned [to this world], he continues until the completion of the first stage (Prathamabhūmi), shining equally upon the six realms of existence as before.
Look! It causes people to feel dread; do not fail to pass through the gateway of birth and death. Believe this word of the Tathāgata’s golden mouth:

with a single mind, recite the Buddha’s name and board the boat to cross over. How fortunate to have now encountered this extraordinary path! With earnest entreaty, I pray that I may soon tread the path of the lotus flowers.
The Eight Sufferings (Introductory Verse):

An account tracing the origins of the eight sufferings begins with human birth. At the moment when the karmic retribution of a dream-like existence comes to an end, the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) does not know which realm it is headed for;
in a state of profound confusion and obscurity, it seizes the vital essence and blood of its parents to undergo conception.
The substance of birth is such that its impure seeds are not beautiful; therefore, this body cannot attain freedom, but is entangled by birth and death in an unbroken chain.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness...
(and so on) ...birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. To speak thus is to encompass the eight sufferings. Old age...
The Master once said: "I have a great affliction: it is because I have this body. If I had no body, what affliction would there be?
However, this does not mean that the absence of a body itself eliminates affliction; rather, it is because the essence is pure and void that afflictions naturally subside.
Therefore, in the land of Amitābha Buddha, beings are born solely through transformation within lotus flowers. Their lifespan is immeasurable;

they are free from all sufferings and enjoy eternal bliss for kalpas. Spontaneously, ignorance is extinguished, whereby volitional formations are extinguished—and so on, until—aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair are extinguished.
Thus, if one truly seeks liberation from the eight kinds of suffering, then the Western Pure Land...
How could one possibly forget the earth for even a moment?

Birth is an error occurring within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) prior to birth itself; it is produced by the three conditions of father and husband, mother and wife. This craving and attachment do not cease and are difficult to grasp.
Seized by the rope of ignorance, they are dragged to the gates of hell and fall into the womb. Even Bodhisattvas are like those covered by a curtain;

when Śrāvakas reach this point, their mental source becomes turbid. How could ordinary sentiments not result in bondage? Knowing this together, take refuge in the fragrant lotus of the Western Pure Land.
Old and worn out, all things are no longer for my enjoyment; reflecting on this, it only increases my grief. May I admonish myself so that I may also admonish the multitude.
This floating life is but a dream. Who knows that the cold and heat will alternate between thawing and freezing? Unaware, Old Yan has already sent his summons. Form...

The divine transformations are difficult to extol; with white hair and wrinkled skin, I bear only sorrow. May the lotus-seed of my heart be shared with those of youthful countenance in the Pure Land of the West.
Illness.
The four elements are in disharmony, violating my physical frame. When ill, who perceives that [suffering] arises in an instant?

Whether sitting or lying down, there is no peace; upon what can one rely? Seek it within yourself. With a sincere heart, recite the Buddha’s name and attend to your health. Break open the skull and examine it closely:
therein, not only is there ultimately nothing of yours, but even this *Saha* world is not it. O Son of Amitābha, the Pure Land lies in the West.
How carefree!
Death is the fruition of the causes of good and evil planted by flowers; as one plants it, so one sits under its shade. When one dies, only one's kin follow.
Rare indeed! There are no permanent locks; heaven and hell are divided by high and low. In the end, the path to the underworld is not to be relied upon.
Why not turn back and renounce it as early as possible? May we firmly hold the rudder of this lotus boat. Within the mind alone, the Western Pure Land is forever secure and peaceful.
The sorrow of parting from those one loves should ultimately return to the essence of non-attachment. This physical body is but a provisional construct;

it may be compared to actors in a troupe of men and women who shed tears in vain. I exhort you all to transcend this cycle together: there must inevitably be separation, for such is the nature of things. Yamen.

In this floating world, who is not subject to death? Since karmic conditions cannot be separated, one must weary of this life. With a heart that rejoices in the Western Pure Land, one shall always be filled with joy.
[Yet,] there is still the meeting with those one hates.
Past karma harbors grievances like two tigers; ten thousand, a hundred thousand, they mutually insult one another. Those who resent gather together in hatred; truly difficult to resist.
Husbands, wives, children, and grandchildren all knit their brows in anger. One can only now cease and desist; such a situation is like the clam and the crab—neither can prevail.
One should believe that the World-Honored One speaks no falsehoods; His compassionate grace is universal throughout the Western Pure Land.
It eliminates all sufferings.

When one seeks what cannot be obtained, one fails to plant the roots of merit for future lives, which is what people hope for. Seeking it and failing to find it adds only to one's despondency; such various causes and conditions are not limited to one.
Thus it is. Be able to know the proper measure; without contention or resentment, frequently practice yielding. Set your mind at ease and cease clinging to appearances.

Do not attempt to dwell long in this Sahā world; realize for yourself that your former efforts have been spent in vain. Return early toward the Western Pure Land, which is universally honored as supreme.
