One thought of Amitābha—the soil is inherently possessed by the mind; To leave the soil and seek the mind is, for the most part, a failure to awaken.
One thought of Amitābha—both doubting and resolving; The self-nature is but the mind; seeing the essential point must be intimate.
A single thought of Amitābha—this conscious spirit is not it; Amitābha and the conscious spirit are both contained within this single, infinitesimal thought.
Amitābha is one's own intrinsic nature; to mistake the conscious spirit for it is a terminal, incurable illness.
A single thought of Amitābha is not an external Buddha; The Amitābha of ten kalpas is a thing within one's own intrinsic nature.
One thought of Amitābha—this directly points to you in this very moment. The true mind and the deluded mind are similar, yet not one and the same.
One thought of Amitābha—this is the pure land of the mind alone. To cling to the mind of reflected images is to mistake the servant for the father.
One thought of Amitābha does not reside within the chest; the Western Pure Land is contained solely within the mind.
A single thought of Amitābha—whether wise or foolish, they differ. The wise seek that land; the foolish cling to it within their own breasts.
A single thought of Amitābha—his face like the sun, his face like the moon; in practice there are east and west, yet in principle there is not a thread’s breadth of separation.
A single thought of Amitābha—vow and vowlessness; it universally encompasses the three faculties, the ultimate fairness and ultimate discourse.
One thought of Amitābha: those of superior faculties have no [separate] vow; having already ascended to the Ten Stages, this is an indeterminate discourse.
One thought of Amitābha: those of middling faculties have no [separate] vow; their delusions and karma are not yet eliminated—this, then, is a mistaken discourse.
One thought of Amitābha: those of inferior faculties have no [separate] vow; they do not know the Pure Land—do not be surprised by such a discourse.
One thought of Amitābha: a mirror for a thousand sages; If you accept it directly, you will surely be deceived.
One thought of Amitābha: a wondrous medicine in sickness; How can one know its flavor? It requires one to chew it thoroughly.
One thought of Amitābha: this is the Supreme Vehicle; If it does not reach before your eyes, you have never realized it.
A single thought of Amitābha— even a fool may practice it. If one believes there is the Western Land, one may entrust oneself to a lotus flower.
A single thought of Amitābha— there is no need for further deliberation. When faith, vow, and practice are complete, one will surely reach the other shore.
A single thought of Amitābha— faith must be vast and great. Rebirth in the Pure Land does not lie outside the mind.
Recite "Nian Amituo" with a vow that is most earnest and deep; within this practice, let joy in the Pure Land and aversion to the defiled realms be sincere in every thought.
Recite "Nian Amituo" with a practice that is single-minded and enduring; even until the moment of death, you must not forget it for a single instant.
Recite "Nian Amituo" as the Samādhi of Single Practice; throughout the twelve periods of the day, keep your focus upon it without retreating.
A single thought of Amitābha— The Buddha has a fundamental vow: If ten thoughts can still lead to birth, How much more so if one does not abandon even a single thought of Amitābha!
Using this as a comparison, That Buddha possesses the affinity; Therefore, exert yourself in a single thought of Amitābha.
Like a single length of white silk, Advance with courage forward, Without needing to turn back your face.
A single thought of Amitābha— The Dharma-realm is of one mark; To advance toward reality is no advancing at all, Yet one advances toward the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
A single thought of Amitābha— Do not fixate on awakening; Simply believe that he is the one to whom you can return. This is the most vital matter.
A single thought of Amitābha— The direct path back to the source, The lotus quarters of the nine grades, Open to both the ordained and the laity.
One thought of Amitābha—may you not err amidst the red dust; Seek rebirth in the Western Land, and never again fall back.
One thought of Amitābha—the name is inscribed upon the lotus calyx; When samādhi is perfected, one returns to their resting place.
One thought of Amitābha—a fine general who repels the enemy; Among the infinite Dharma gates, none surpasses this.
One thought of Amitābha—do not be complacent; exert yourself to bring it forth and sever the myriad threads of delusion.
One thought of Amitābha—transcend the wheel of suffering; for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, you shall no longer endure bitter pain.
One thought of Amitābha—your pure karma will be equal to that of the sages; do not discriminate between right and wrong, and yield fame and profit to others.
One thought of Amitābha—neither difficult nor easy; Provided one attains single-mindedness, the supreme excellence is naturally complete.
What is the meaning of "one thought of Amitābha"? The more focused, the more unified; do not seek it elsewhere.
"One thought of Amitābha" is inconceivable; It is most sudden and most perfect, most simple and most easy.
One thought of Amitābha—now is precisely the time. Upon this path, do not entertain further doubt.
One thought of Amitābha is the practice for the末世 (final age); if one wishes to leave the realms of suffering, there is only rebirth in the Pure Land.
One thought of Amitābha—exhort and protect yourself at all times; until you have attained rebirth, how could you avoid anxiety and fear?
One thought of Amitābha—cherish this one crucial point. When the time of departure arrives, by no means retreat.
One thought of Amitābha must be held with joyful earnestness; the splendors of Sukhāvatī are manifested according to the mind.
One thought of Amitābha must be held with weary earnestness; the eight sufferings burn together, leaving no place from which to escape.
One thought of Amitābha: the essential is that the mind be earnest; simply seek liberation, and the Saha world will be instantly severed.
One thought of Amitābha: the essential is that the recitation be earnest; bring forth the Great Name, biting through the nail and chewing through the iron.
One thought of Amitābha: the essential is that the focus be earnest; simply prepare a heart of resolve, and there is no other secret instruction.
The Nian Amituo: the essential point lies in its intensity; With a body like a collapsing mountain, one must cast oneself in sincerity with tears of blood.
The Nian Amituo: furthermore, it lies in the intensity of faith; One must kick over the mass of doubt until it is shattered into pieces.
The Nian Amituo: furthermore, it lies in the intensity of the vow; One must resolutely await rebirth, without turning toward other paths.
A single thought of Amitābha—(the "n" in *yì* is pronounced with the *xíng* tone)— Even if the fires at the end of the kalpa should break out, The mind shall not change its course.
A single thought of Amitābha— The response is like a shadow; The original essence is empty. Thus one rejoices and feels fortunate.
A single thought of Amitābha— The Buddha is made by the mind; The lotus pedestal awaits in the air, Guiding one back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In a single thought of Amitābha, the transformation Buddha adorns the crown; beyond the Buddha there is no mind, and beyond the mind there is no object.
In a single thought of Amitābha, the jeweled vase atop the topknot is nothing other than this: it is the numinous power inherently possessed.
In a single thought of Amitābha, he pervades all of empty space; this entire assembly of the ocean-like multitude is neither different nor the same.
In a single thought of Amitābha, the Immovable Bodhimanda; Without departing from this very thought, one has already gone to the Western Land.
In a single thought of Amitābha, the jewel pond flowers bloom; One realizes the patience of non-arising and beholds the Tathāgata face-to-face.
In a single thought of Amitābha, turning oneself toward others; The ten bodies are perfectly manifested, universally transforming the Sahā world.
A single thought of Amitābha is the essential task for benefiting sentient beings; The self-nature is boundless, and all sentient beings are equally delivered.
A single thought of Amitābha fulfills the vow of Bodhi; The self-nature is inexhaustible, and afflictions are suddenly severed.
A single thought of Amitābha is perfect enlightenment; The self-nature is immeasurable, and its Dharma-gate transcends study.
A single thought of Amitābha is eternally quiescent and luminous; The supreme self-nature brings the Buddha-way to perfect completion.
A single thought of Amitābha is the realm of non-action; Whether saint or ordinary being, there is no need for further effort.
A single thought of Amitābha is transmitted through eternal kalpas; I only pray that all sentient beings may ascend together to the Land of Bliss.
A Question on Single-minded Practice for Rebirth (with Preface):
The *Wen shu* states: "One who captures birds uses a net; one cannot call a single eye of the net 'a net.
One who governs a state relies on the merit of a single person; one cannot call a single person 'the state. Now, the Pure Land should be likewise. Why is this not so?"
If all virtues are equally perfumed, how can one be singled out as having attained rebirth? My answer to this question has not yet reached its essential point. Why is this?
It is because the single gate of the Pure Land depends entirely upon faith and aspiration. If faith and aspiration are complete, one will attain rebirth even through scattered recitation.

But if faith and aspiration are lacking, can one attain birth merely through the assistance of myriad practices? [The questioner asks: "What are faith and aspiration? [The master replies: "It is to believe in this..."
Where there is birth, there must be death; within the cycle of birth and death, no one can escape the various sufferings.

Furthermore, I believe that in that land, one need not discard this body to receive another until reaching the stage of the "Successor to Buddhahood" (Upapadya-bhūmi), constantly experiencing bliss throughout the interval.
Moreover, I vow that this turbid and defiled body shall be decisively abandoned and never received again, and that I shall instead attain that pure and ethereal form.
If one makes a firm resolve that their ultimate reliance shall never change, and if the fruit is indeed attained as such, then even the simultaneous cultivation of the myriad virtues will arise;
how much more so for merely reciting the Name?
When study reaches the stage of no-mind, one aspires for rebirth; throughout one's life, one takes refuge and upholds the Name. Know that my transgressions and those of others are equal.
Let all hear this with one mind and refrain from dispute altogether.

As they speak on and on, let them speak of holding the Name. Ask me, and I shall surely provide the method within it. For sentient beings burdened by many obstacles, the practice of Buddha-remembrance and visualization is the easiest path to reach the Long Star (Venus) in this present age.
Severing doubt and giving rise to faith, one’s resolve shall be firm; day after day, remaining thus, one shall not change the strings.
I only hope that at the moment of death, I shall return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, with no other matters to entangle me.
Having studied the direct pointing of the Dharma before, I have come to know that reciting the Buddha's name is superior to practicing Zen. Zen involves suffering from beginning to end;
in the Pure Land, the fruits of the Way are perfected in a single lifetime.
May all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm together attain [liberation] (with preface).

The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Sentient beings are the pure land of the bodhisattva. Thus we know that when a bodhisattva practices mindfulness of the Buddha, it is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings and not for their own sake.
Although they spend their entire day saving sentient beings, it is as if they were saving themselves. Throughout the day...
To recollect the Buddha is still to recollect oneself. Why is this? Because for a Bodhisattva there is no self and nothing that is not the self;
they have realized that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are without distinction. It is like the sky universally covering, or like the earth universally supporting.

To abandon sentient beings is to abandon oneself; to distance oneself from the Buddha is to distance oneself from the mind. Yet the mind cannot be distanced, and sentient beings cannot be abandoned. This is what Yunmen meant by "the casket."
That which covers heaven and earth—how could its essential meaning transcend this?

Bowing my head amidst the flowers, I take refuge in the Buddha amidst the flowers; may we together with those amidst the flowers form the holy embryo (*garbha*). In that land, there is no birth, yet one departs all day long;

the Honored Countenance does not move, yet it arrives in response to the moment. Having cast off the skeletal remains of the red dust of the sea of suffering, they are transformed into the white lotuses of a precious pond.
Jade Child. Recorded as having made a pact together with the Sahā world. Throughout the ten directions, all are purple-golden terraces.
A Warning on Habitual Tendencies and Exhortation to Practice (with preface):
That which is most difficult for us to eradicate is habitual tendency (*vāsanā*). Although there is no skillful means to sever it, one must not... [omit]... fail to do so.
One should allow what has been formed through habituation to take its course, yet one must certainly strive so that one's practice does not become lax.

Why is this? When the World-Honored One ascended the stages in the past, he had only recently served the ancient Śākyamuni; at that time, he was still abiding in the rank of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha said that in past lives, I was also once an evil person or a small insect; it was because of the accumulation of merit that I [attained this]."
Thus he attained Buddhahood. Judging from this, even at the tenth stage there still remain the dual habits of mind and form; how much more so for the stages below?
Had he not exerted himself in practice at that time, how could he have attained Buddhahood today?

Having already realized the nature of the deep-seated habitual afflictions, one should exert oneself and strive in practice from within one's own home. Neither departing from nor adhering to them, one makes their substance empty;
thus, with a single mind, one’s knowledge and vision accord with that of the Buddha to effect healing.
Though one knows that the essence of this defiled land is the same [as the Pure Land], if one loses illumination for even a moment, one will be obscured from the true void.
Only after waiting for them to go and behold Amitābha can one then sport and roam within the hells.

The five desires pull one toward falling into the fiery pit; the master must guard them closely and not follow emotional impulses. Observe that the four great elements are originally without substance;
do not follow conditions and thus incur rebirth.
The ultimate cessation of the conditions of defilement is the cause for their future emergence; it is simply the Lotus Vow that desires intimacy.
On the path where the same essence ascends and sinks through the realms of ordinary beings and sages, as soon as a thought arises, look into its true nature yourself.
Mutually, they were originally empty from the start; before their distinction was made, all was dim and obscure. In the West, both mind and land are pure;
compared to this Sahā world, they are vastly different.

After awakening, one must know that craving must be severed of its own accord. Do not forget the suffering of birth and death—how lamentable! Though the mind is empty and still, it is ultimately difficult to endure;
one must surely return to preserve the sacred embryo.
A Severe Exhortation to Rebirth (with Preface):
Since beginningless time, having been born we have died again; having died, we have been born again. Birth after birth, death after death—we have not yet escaped this cycle to this day.
What is the reason for this? It is solely due to the two characters "habitual negligence" (*yin-xun*), which has led us to suffer through rebirth in vain.
All sufferings. For this reason, in the past, there was one named Zhang Zuliu.

A friend exhorted him to practice *nianfo* for rebirth in the Pure Land, but Zuliu said, "My son is not yet married, my daughter is not yet wedded, and my parents' coffins have not yet been interred. Shortly thereafter, he passed away.

His friend went to offer condolences and said, "My friend's name was Zhang Zuliu; I exhorted him to practice *nianfo*, yet he spoke of three heads [of unfulfilled duties]. How strange that the Lord of Yama!"
There is no clarity. Before the three heads are even resolved, one is already hooked. Thus we know that those who cultivate the practice of purity must not be too lax;
a single error leads to a hundred errors.
In the age of the final dharma, people must face birth and death; among billions of brave warriors, who can prevail?
Know that one may escape from the turbulent sea of suffering, as is very clearly set forth in the *Candragarbha-sūtra*.
I exhort you to uphold the Name without waiting for the time; those who seek rebirth must first know this for themselves. In this Jambudvīpa world, the span of life is short;
one only fears that in the end, it will be too late through error and delay.

Life exists only in the breath; do not slacken in your cultivation. Just look at what Master Zhang left behind in his day. Worldly affairs are like a game of chess, difficult to bring to a conclusion;
prepare your provisions early and board the returning boat.
The fruits of causes and conditions from pure karma do not fail; the single path home leads through the slanting evening sun.
Though other gates are indeed all capable of entry, none is as stable and secure as the excellence of Buddha-recitation.

If for even one breath you do not return, you will follow the stream of karma. Recite the Buddha's name with sincerity; do not be hypocritical. It would be like ascending a precious mountain peak only to return empty-handed;
regret is difficult to overcome, leading only to self-worry.
Those who have not yet attained a heart of refuge must not rest complacent; those who have already begun their practice of vows must not slacken further.
If one merely rides upon the karmic conditions of this world for another lifetime, the desire to attain liberation will be the most difficult of difficulties.
Like dousing a fire on one's head, this concerns only oneself; when hungry, one eats rice—how could it concern another?
Even if one claims that earth is the purity of the mind-only, how can it compare to the fact that rebirth in the Pure Land is even more true?
Regarding the dedication of merit at the time of death (with an introductory note):
Those who already know how to seek rebirth in the Pure Land should not allow their minds to become too anxious. The essential point is simply to neither cling nor distance oneself from the practice.
Take, for example, Master Faying, who clarified the mind and the Pure Land for thirty years; or Vinaya Master Huiheng, who [practiced] for six... [years].
For ten years, one must seek with single-minded purity. Yet people today often possess shallow views;

upon hearing in detail that when the time for reciting the Buddha’s name has not yet reached one or two years, or even eight or ten years, the pure realm has not yet become uniform and the various texts on the Pure Lands have not yet been carefully and thoroughly studied, they fail to know its flavor.
They then claim to change their tune and retreat from the practice. How could this be?
To hope for the realization of the Way through mere contemplation—when will that day ever come? Thus, the former scholars had a saying:
"One must not, because benevolence is difficult to mature, willingly accept that other paths have already achieved success. This was precisely what they meant.

Furthermore, as for the essentials of the Pure Land, regardless of whether one has sharp or dull faculties, whether one is a long-time practitioner or a beginner, or whether one is in a state of stillness or not—all are verified at the moment of death.
Finally, you shall attain it; let this be your true deadline. Any further desire to seek awakening or to develop wisdom is neither urgent nor essential.
Therefore, I say to my fellow students who come after: since you have already entered this extraordinary gate, remain firm in your resolve and do not waver.
In seeking the Way, there is nothing else to deliberate upon; it all depends on the practitioner’s own resolve. Minor skills are mastered through proficiency;
do not allow the Great Matter to lose its singular excellence.

Throughout my life, I have had nothing left but the hope of returning to the West. With absolute certainty and without doubt, may my vow not be thwarted. A mere snap of the fingers can transcend the realm of pure dreams;
it is hundreds of thousands of millions of times faster than flight.

When the merit of samādhi is perfected, one casts off the hand and returns home; as one departs, the Buddha-light naturally surrounds them. To brood over the past and worry about the future is but a waste of effort;
one simply must sever the notions of right and wrong.
Only when one’s principle accords with reality does one know the skill of the path; at the critical pass of birth and death, the merit of Chan meditation triumphs.
How many those who possess eloquence like a cascading river fail to equal the simple woman who persevered in holding the Name until her end.
If one commits evil, one will be reborn as Zhang Shanhe; those who speak of their goodness are even more numerous. For the most part, this is invariably the case;
the crucial point lies in that single kṣaṇa at the moment of death.
Having gained entry through this gate by virtue of past roots of goodness, my efforts are now complete as I emerge from the universe.
As a man of the wilds, I vow to offer lotus flowers, separately repaying the grace of the prophecies bestowed upon me by the ten directions.
Who has ever known the Pure Land of Mind-only? What is precious is the time when there is no longer any falling back.
It is best to return to it in this very life, so as to avoid further wandering through the prison of the womb.
Cultivating pure practice is itself true emptiness; when the dream ends upon a single pillow, the path naturally opens. Father and son are intimately connected as he personally hands it over;
rebirth occurs, as ever, within the wondrous mind.
An Essential Summary of the Pure Land (with Preface) I have heard that since the time of Bodhidharma,
those who pride themselves on the power of their own effort in Chan meditation have been numerous, yet those who place their faith and take refuge in the Pure Land have been few.
How few there have ever been! Alas! Even Yunmen, who thrice served as a king, ultimately lost his supernatural powers;
how much more so for those of lesser intelligence? For to lose them is to regress. As the *Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"All those born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*). When compared by this standard, which is more beneficial: Chan or Pure Land? Can [you say]?
However, this is clearly evident; thus, the *Liaojian* says: "If there is Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray. This is truly lamentable.
One should know that for practice in the Dharma-ending age, unless one relies on the Western Pure Land to achieve horizontal transcendence through both principle and phenomena, [success is unlikely].

If one seeks those who do not fall back or regress, they can ultimately never be found. If one is indeed able to have deep faith in this, then the supreme dignity of the Pure Land Dharma-door leaves no room for delay or hesitation.
Because I am free from shame, I have divided the subject matter and composed this work;

furthermore, I append these twenty [verses] as an exhortation to practice, intended to serve as a warning against complacency and to encourage joy in the pure and revulsion toward the defiled, as well as faith, aspiration, conduct, mindfulness, and contemplation through sustained and focused application.
The foremost words of summary, addressed with sincerity to those of lofty intelligence:

The World-Honored One of the Western Pure Land personally pointed this out, out of compassion for us in the final age, to rescue us from the perilous straits of delusion, bringing us all onto the boat within the sea of suffering.

Guest: We are fellow practitioners at the Lotus Pond Assembly; even our names are not heard in the three evil realms. These flowers can constantly rain down anew throughout the six periods of the day.
The beings born here are inconceivable; many possess the bodies of those destined for Buddhahood in their next life.

Now that I have faith in the Long-Eared Star (Venus), it shall surely not err. I constantly contemplate that land, the Dharma-king’s realm, where fragrances are woven among the flowers as the fruit of the mind-lake, and branches sprout upon the banks as the buds of the Way-tree.
My longing to rely upon the Lotus Throne is uniquely intense; may I be guided back like a sunflower seed held in the hand.
Frequently leaning toward the west, one’s vow to benefit sentient beings will ultimately be fulfilled. The perfected manifestation-body is like a mist emerging from a mountain peak;

the pure, all-pervading true body has neither coming nor going. May the precious pond lend me its waters to wash away the dust of defilement; may the depths and shallows of the water's flow follow my heart’s intent.
Desire: Red and white flower branches bloom with every thought. A precious canopy covers the void for the Great Being of Gold; fragrant clouds swirl around the infant of Jade.
Within the coral trees, atop the crystal towers, all are of the same kind as they nurture the sacred embryo.

The Western Pure Land of the Earth is my own mind; the pervasive sandy yellow ground is gold. Branches rising from the water support round leaves above, while fragrant shores surround deep lotus flowers.
Through the pearl of precepts, one suddenly awakens to the patience of non-arising, frequently hearing the wondrous songs of birds.
The Dharma-sound has been transmitted across vast distances by successive virtuous friends; may all kinsmen and followers together return to it.

Do not flee from principle to seek meditation, nor allow the chest to be recognized as the self. Amitābha of one's own nature comes to visit you from afar; he and you are never separate, even while remaining distinct.
From beginning to end, it is neither ancient nor modern; the perfectly integrated essence of awakening is always thus. Encompassing all of space, what need is there to seek it?
Unified and singular, it penetrates vertically and pervades horizontally; in every atom and every world-system lies the wondrously luminous mind.

The compassionate decree of the Dharma King is not transmitted in vain; there truly are matters of the Western Land, as vivid as they were before. May my lifespan and years be eternal like the Buddha’s;
may the garments and food I desire appear before me. The patterns of the clouds reflect upon the balustrades, and the sounds of music return with the wind as I walk.
Beside the trees, joy and carefree wandering never end; returning, we sit together upon the lotuses of the Jade Pond.
Transversely across the three realms, a single path is opened; it leads me back easily to my native home to rest. Within this, one recites the Buddha’s name and yearns for kin.

In this place, names are inscribed upon flowers as they enter the ranks of the assembly. May you swiftly realize Bodhi so that there is no further existence; may you soon awaken from former delusions in the Pure Land.
The Compassionate Honored One has long waited for you on the other shore; once you let go, you shall immediately be like a horse’s hoof resting upon it.
Transcending desire, one attains transcendence of birth and liberation from death; with a mind of weary detachment toward the Sahā world, one approaches the land of the Original Amitāyus Buddha.
All therein are persons of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*); for ten thousand kalpas, the springtime of adornments never fades, and a thousand flowers are embroidered in boundless colors.
Ever-new is the path; when the fruit of practice is fulfilled on the Golden Ground, one attains a world-transcending body therein.

I urge you to follow this shortcut toward the West without delay; cast aside body and mind and pass through [to liberation] early. Fame and profit are originally empty—do not remain attached even to them.

Renunciation! When death and rebirth are already upon us, what is to be done? Through the sincere practice of the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one truly moves the Buddha to appear at the moment of death.
By relying on this, one is liberated from beginningless saṃsāra; only then does one realize that the Pure Land is distinct from this Sahā world.
Cultivating both joy and aversion, these two aspects strike at one another; that land lies afar, yet the path to it opens of itself. It is the place where all superior virtuous people gather;
among them, excellent friends fill the void. Seeing through the red dust of the world, it is like a mere play; having cultivated pure deeds, one is already advanced.
Emerging from the cage, we realize that in this land the body is easily lost; together we return to see the Buddha, whose life-span is infinite.

Rejoicing in the Land of Bliss, I point to its excellence as surpassing all others; forever severing the cycle of rebirth, we escape suffering and toil, boarding the ship of great vows to return to our original home.
Filling the entire realm of empty space, the whole body manifests; its many wondrous forms are as pure as jade, and its countless lotus varieties are equally precious.
Such is the mind alone, such is the objective realm; thus do the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises proceed.

One loathes the impurity of the capital city and speaks of worldly relations; one undergoes the exhaustion and torment of the eight sufferings. Earth, water, fire, and wind compose this illusory body;
one grieves over joy and sorrow, parting and meeting, clinging to this floating form. One strives vainly in the empty fray of self and others, mistakenly guarding against flaws and blemishes.
Recognize this treasure! Turn back early; there is a pressing need for deep weariness [with saṃsāra]. Sever the rope of delusion; do not remain complacent.
Trust in the Great Name and raise your will toward the Western Land. Establish your faith and keep your feet steady; do not waver. The Lotus Sea’s compassion is profound—grant me entry.

Entering [the Way], with sincere devotion and faith, I desire for you to transcend [suffering]. The crow and the wheel are recalled afar as they fall toward the edge of the sky; the golden arm is difficult to forget as it beckons within a dream.
When the earth is realized as one’s own mind, the return is secure; the karma of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas can be extinguished.
May I have little concern for the myriad affairs of the world; my aim is to travel the path back to the source. When the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is deep, the vast ocean seems shallow;

when the vow for rebirth is heavy, Mount Tai seems light. One who has not yet perfected the power of patience should believe in purity; one who has already traversed kalpas of the bodhisattva path need only maintain faith.
Just as he was about to depart, he burned incense morning and evening and prostrated himself, making this vow: "May I reach my native city early upon my journey.

While traveling, may there be no birth and all doubts be severed. Ten thousand oxen cannot restrain me from galloping westward; I shall transcend horizontally across three thousand worlds of this Sahā realm."
The realms revolve like a wheel of beads through the twelve hours; in every thought-moment, this mind attains the pinnacle of emptiness. In every sound, that self-nature is Amitābha.
Reaching the precious pond together, we receive his personal touch upon our crowns; come now to act as the masters who select Buddhas through their manifold emanations.

Contemplating the Great Being within the visualization, attending upon Amitābha— Ordinary and sage beings are fundamentally one in essence, without partiality. A single white hair between the brows emits light, serene and vast;
The breeze is clear by the pond’s edge, the environment harmonious and peaceful. Red petals flutter up and down like thousands of layers of cotton; Green waves swell from east to west as one.
The samādhi is fully perfected; the primary and secondary realms are established. Since this mind itself creates the Buddha, how could there be any confusion?

Whether the spirit is in a state of stillness or distraction, do not concern yourself with such distinctions. With every sound, call forth the original reality. Take wide strides upon the Great Path and return to the West.
The path: Do not seek wonders elsewhere or ask for other crossings. With doubt severed, you will surely reach the goal; through uninterrupted practice, it becomes naturally pure.

(Whenever one hears a Chan practitioner ask, "Ultimately, who is this 'one'? they themselves do not know. They tend to suppress beginners by asking, "Who exactly is this person who recites the Buddha's name? One should answer: Relying on his recitation, who shall be my master?
I only wish to be reborn in the Pure Land and leave the mundane world behind.

Single-mindedly and with focused diligence, recite the Buddha’s name to transcend the clamor of the mundane world. Fix the number of recitations and do not let them slacken. The nature of the Name is empty, yet its sound is distinct and clear;
this is the direct path home, long and far-reaching. Know that it is like entering alone on horseback with a single blade; one has not yet seen the three minds or two [delusions].
The mind transcends. Even if one’s practice is deep, let it rest naturally without obstruction. The Compassionate Honored One can grant forgiveness; rebirth will be achieved as obstacles dissolve.
To long dwell in the Pure Land, holding the Name is the most easy way to transcend. Do not allow your heels to be shaken by others. Be solely focused and attentive; thus your merit will increase.

Victorious! The longer it lasts, the firmer it becomes, and the more abundant it grows. There was once a vow for the depth of compassion in ten recitations; how could there be no solace in the piercing urgency of a single lifetime?
That which is reached by a mere snap of the fingers is fundamentally of the same essence; thus it is said that the path to the Western Land is not remote.

[The Warning: Although one has already grown weary [of the world], one must vow to remain until the end of life. Alas, the fragile vessel has not yet been fired; defiled and evil conditions are powerful. One must issue a further warning before one can succeed in reaching the final goal.
Not having yet reached the ancient shore is most lamentable; once the human body is lost, the path becomes ever more remote.

Only now, after kalpas of vast eons, have I finally awakened; from this birth onward, there shall be no returning to error. Firm and steadfast pure vows require no external force; one must strenuously spur oneself toward pure cultivation.
My own home. To exhaustively investigate the secular world, one finds it ultimately perilous; to resign oneself to the return to Sukhāvatī, one is as flawless as jade.
The Ritual for the Pure Land (with Preface):

Originally, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, it was nothing other than for the sake of benefiting and rescuing others. If the Dharma were not transmitted by the sages, how could living beings be benefited?
Therefore, we know that what the Tathāgata preaches is that there is nothing preached; yet it fully explains that which sentient beings practice.
Sentient beings practice that which is not practiced, and they fully practice that which the Tathāgata has preached. This is an immutable thesis established for all eternity.

If it were otherwise, one would merely be refining the fabrications of one's own imagination; such effort would surely be in vain, and with the persistence of birth and extinction, what benefit would there be for humanity?
This is truly because the source of awakening is vast and boundless, and the ocean of nature is expansive and deep; it cannot be reached without following a guiding compass.
Those who do not become confused regarding the four directions are rare indeed. Thus, the *Protocol for the Capital* states:

"To take refuge in the Triple Gem is essentially to point toward a direction and establish a sign, causing the mind to dwell upon and grasp at an object; it does not clarify the signless state that is free from thought.

The Buddha knew in advance that even when ordinary beings fixate their minds [on a sign], they still fail; how much more so, then, would they fail to be free from signs? Therefore, those of my same class seek rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Regarding the "Western Quarter": this is where one should establish this ritual procedure (*vidhi*). What is this ritual procedure?

Within the hall of offerings, one must install a Buddha image facing east while seated westward; only then may one begin the practice. In this way, it perfectly accords with the Buddha’s intention, as stated in the Sūtra:
"From this Western Quarter, passing through hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī..."
Joyful! In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma.

It is because I have seen these benefits that I have spoken these words and other such exhortations. Since it is stated that one must travel west from here, it is clear that the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) is certainly located to the west.
Now, even the upright and virtuous gentlemen of this world do not utter false speech to deceive others; how much less so [would the Buddhas]?
The Tathāgata who has transcended the world has personally transmitted this with his golden mouth; how could there be any falsehood to deceive me?

Viewing it in this light, such a thing is certainly impossible. Therefore, one must believe that in the Western Quarter there truly exist such lotus-buddha lands where the wind-stirred branches produce the sound of music and the precious ponds’ water-birds proclaim the precious scriptures. Once born in those lands, all shall never regress from the path. Relying upon...
Indeed, these various forms stand forth in majestic array, their sublime beauty transcending all; compared to the turbid world, they are vastly unequal.
We ought naturally to look upon them with joy and reverence. Even if the specific location is not yet fixed, the sacred images will remain peaceful and oriented wherever they are placed.

Furthermore, one must never depart from the West in one's contemplation. Why is this? It is because ordinary beings in the mundane world have the "monkey of the mind" without a master and the "horse of the will" that has forgotten its way home;
if they do not rely on that Dharma King to guide them, it is difficult to aspire to return.
It is, for example, like a noble youth seeking fame: if he does not rely on our Imperial Lord to select him, it is difficult to succeed in the examination. Therefore, [the selection...]
The official must surely receive the grace of the North; to seek the Buddha, one should turn westward. Therefore, those who cultivate the Pure Land must not lack ritual form.
It is like a strategy for resisting an enemy: when the formation is formidable, the rebel army retreats of its own accord without being attacked.
Likewise, when the method of holding the Name is strict in its ritual, deluded habits vanish of their own accord without needing to be eliminated. Thus, I exhort you to recite it.

The Buddha. Having performed prostrations, repentance, and made vows for dedication, may all—monastics and laypeople alike, old and young, wise and foolish, rich and poor, male and female—each and every one believe in this.
May they follow these rites throughout the day;

thus, it is hoped that my mind and state will become easily focused, pure mindfulness will not be forgotten, and through long-term practice without cessation, once the conditions reach full maturity, we shall together ascend to the realm of purity and peace.
Thus it is said in the *Xiāng* (Local Records).

△ Morning Ten Recitations (As for the method of the ten recitations, it was established by the Venerable Master Ciyun. Every morning, having dressed, face directly west, join the palms and settle the mind, and recite the names as follows):
Homage to Amitābha Buddha, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One, the Teacher who Welcomes and Guides with Great Vows and Great Power, in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Amitābha Buddha.

(Exhaling a single breath constitutes one recitation. Ten such breaths are called ten recitations. One simply follows the length of the breaths without limiting the number of Buddhas; the breaths are completed as they end. The sound should be neither too high nor too low, neither too slow nor too fast, but balanced in the middle.

Ten breaths are linked together so that the mind does not scatter, making this focused application the merit. What is called "ten recitations" is thus using the breath to bind the mind. Having made these recitations, one makes a vow of dedication, saying:)
I, disciple [Name], with single-minded devotion take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
May you illuminate me with your pure light and embrace me with your compassionate vows. Now, with right mindfulness, I invoke the name of the Tathāgata;
for the sake of the path to Bodhi, I seek birth in the Pure Land. According to the Buddha’s original vow: "If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in my land... [and so forth].

With a heart of faith and joy, even for ten recitations—if I do not attain birth [in that land], may I not realize perfect enlightenment, except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma.
As I now recall, from this life onward, I have committed no karmic offenses and have not slandered the Mahāyāna.
May these ten recitations enable me to enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows; by riding upon the power of the Buddha’s compassion, may all my transgressions be extinguished and purified.

Through this cause, [merit] increases. When the end of life approaches, one knows in advance that the time has come; the body is free from the suffering of illness, the mind is free from attachment, and the consciousness is free from delusion.

As if entering meditative absorption, the Buddhas and the assembly of sages arrive to welcome me, holding golden platforms in their hands. In the space of a single thought-moment, I am reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Upon the opening of the lotus flower, I behold the Buddha and immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle, whereby the wisdom of the Buddha is suddenly and fully opened. Extensively...
To deliver all sentient beings and fulfill the vow for Bodhi.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas: [I take refuge in] the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

(Having made this vow, it is acceptable whether one bows to the Buddha or not; however, one must not abandon it for even a single day throughout this entire life. By simply ensuring it is not abandoned, and by personally restraining one's own mind, one shall attain birth in that land.)

△ Next, the Rite of Prostration and Repentance (Now, those who seek rebirth in the Western Land must necessarily perform this rite of repentance in conjunction with their practice. It should be performed regularly as the morning service. Within one’s usual place of offerings, maintain an upright and reverent demeanor; join the palms and settle the mind, and speak as follows).

With all reverence, single-mindedly prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem (keeping in mind that one is universally prostrating to all the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Treasures of the ten directions and the three periods of time). Upon rising from the prostration, kneel with both knees on the ground and hold an incense burner in your hands.
(Burning clouds of various famous incenses:
May these clouds of incense and flowers fill the realms of the ten directions, adorning the infinite Buddha-fields with immeasurable fragrances.
I fulfill the Bodhisattva path and achieve the fragrance of the Tathāgata.

(This incense and flower of mine pervades the ten directions, serving as a subtle and wondrous light-pavilion. With celestial music and divine precious incense, with celestial delicacies and divine precious robes, and with inconceivable particles of the sublime Dharma—each particle giving rise to all particles, each particle giving rise to all dharmas—they revolve without obstruction, mutually adorning one another.
Reaching before the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the Dharma-realm, in every instance there is my own body performing offerings. Each and every one...

Pervading the entire dharma-realm, they are distinct yet without obstruction in each respective place; throughout the limits of the future, they perform the buddha-work, universally suffusing all sentient beings within the dharma-realm. Having been suffused by this, all give rise to the bodhicitta and together enter the non-arising state to realize buddha-wisdom.
Having made these offerings, with all reverence,
I prostrate now before the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body, which is peerless in the world, incomparable, and inconceivable.
The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so; all phenomena are eternally abiding—therefore, I take refuge.
Through the power of great wisdom and great vows, he universally delivers all sentient beings, causing them to cast off their bodies of feverish affliction and be born in that land of cool serenity.
I now purify my three karmas; taking refuge and offering praise, I vow that together with all sentient beings, we may be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
(Having completed this praise and vow, one should immediately prostrate to the Buddha, focusing the mind one-pointedly upon each instance and saying:)

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. To the one who widely propagates the Pure Land of Bliss, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and his thousands of billions of transformation bodies—the Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma realm.
(Bowing down, gaze upward and say:)

The worshiper and the object of worship both proceed into emptiness and stillness; the resonance between them is inconceivable. My *bodhimaṇḍa* is like a jewel of Indra, within which the shadow-forms of Śākyamuni Buddha appear. My own shadow-form appears before Śākyamuni Buddha; I pray for rebirth there to prostrate at his feet.
[In the following sections, simply change the name of the honored one according to the respective stage. Regarding the visualization for the prostrations, it is said as follows: etc.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Amitābha Tathāgata of the eternally quiescent and luminous Pure Land, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body that pervades all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Amitābha Tathāgata of the truly retributive adorned land, the body of a sea of subtle-dust marks that pervades...

With a single mind, I prostrate to all Buddhas of the Dharma-realm. To Amitābha Tathāgata, who dwells in the land of skillful means, whose body is adorned with the marks of liberation, and who pervades all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm.

With one mind, I prostrate to the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss. With one mind, I prostrate to all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm, who are the root, realm, and body of the Mahāyāna.

With one mind, I prostrate to the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss, whose emanated bodies travel to the ten directions. With one mind, I prostrate to all [Buddhas] throughout...

The Honored Dharma is extolled throughout the entire Dharma-realm. (The True Emptiness of Dharmatā is like space; my body manifests before the Dharma-treasure. The eternally abiding Dharma-treasure is inconceivable; I pray for rebirth there and take refuge in prostration.)
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whose ten billion bodies of purple-gold pervade the entire Dharma-realm,
and to all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. With single-minded devotion,
I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whose body of infinite light and wisdom pervades...

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-realm pay homage with single-minded devotion. To the Western Land of Peace and Bliss; to the assembly of the pure great ocean; to those whose bodies are perfected by the two types of adornment;

to the holy assembly pervading the entire Dharma-realm. (Having finished the prostration, kneeling on both knees, holding the hand-incense burner and burning incense, they speak these words with utmost sincerity:)

I now universally act for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, those in the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm; may we all vow to sever the three obstacles and take refuge through repentance.

From beginningless time until the present, I and all sentient beings, due to craving and false views, have internally clung to the notions of self and person and externally associated with evil friends. We have failed to rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of another’s goodness, but rather, throughout our three karmic faculties, we have extensively committed grave offenses.

Although his transgressions were not extensive, his evil intent was pervasive, continuing day and night without interruption. He concealed his faults and did not wish for others to know them; he feared neither the evil realms nor felt shame or remorse, and he denied the existence of cause and effect. Therefore, on this day—

I deeply believe in cause and effect. I give rise to profound shame and remorse, and I conceive great fear. I reveal and repent my transgressions, severing the continuity of such thoughts. I resolve to attain Bodhicitta, abandoning evil and cultivating good. I urge on my three karmas to overturn my past grave offenses.

I rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of merit performed by ordinary beings or sages alike. I contemplate the Buddhas of the ten directions, who possess great merit and wisdom, and are able to rescue and deliver me and all sentient beings from the sea of the two deaths, placing us upon the shore of the three virtues. From time immemorial, I have not known that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent.

I have extensively committed many evils. Now, knowing emptiness and stillness, for the sake of seeking Bodhi and for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall extensively cultivate all virtues and universally sever all evils. I only pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the World-Honored One Amitābha will compassionately accept me and grant me leave to repent.

I prostrate with all my heart and repent. I, your disciple [Name], together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, from time immemorial until now, have been shrouded by ignorance and deluded by inverted views.

Through the six sense organs and the three karmas, we have practiced unwholesome dharmas and extensively committed the ten evil deeds, the five acts of immediate retribution, and all manner of transgressions—immeasurable, boundless, and beyond description throughout the ten directions.
The Buddhas always abide within the world; the sound of the Dharma never ceases. Wondrous fragrances fill all space, and the flavor of the Dharma overflows the void.
They emit pure radiance that illuminates and touches all things; the eternally abiding sublime principle pervades the entirety of empty space.

Yet, from time immemorial, my six sense organs have been internally blind and my three karmas shrouded in darkness. I have neither seen nor heard, neither awakened nor known. By these causes and conditions, I have long drifted in the current.
They undergo birth and death, traversing the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas without any prospect of escape. A sutra states that Vairocana pervades all places;
the dwelling place of that Buddha is called the Light of Eternal Quiescence. Therefore, one should know that all dharmas [are thus].
There is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma, yet I did not understand this; I followed the flow of ignorance.
Thus, within Bodhi I saw impurity, and within liberation I gave rise to fetters. Now I have finally awakened; now I have finally repented.
I prostrate myself before you in homage.
I confess and repent before all Buddhas and the World-Honored One Amitābha.

May it cause me and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm—regarding all grave offenses committed through the three karmas and six sense faculties from beginningless time, whether currently committed, to be committed, or already committed; whether performed by myself, taught to others, or rejoiced in upon seeing or hearing them;
whether remembered or forgotten, recognized or unrecognized, doubted or not doubted, concealed or revealed—to bring them all to ultimate end.
Purity! Having repented, my six sense organs and three karmas are pure and free from blemish or defilement. All roots of goodness I have cultivated are likewise pure;
I dedicate them all to adorn the Pure Land and to be born together with all sentient beings in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
I pray that Amitābha Buddha will constantly come to protect and sustain me, causing my roots of goodness to increase before me, so that I shall not lose the cause of purity.
At the time of death, my body and mind shall be possessed of right mindfulness, my sight and hearing shall be clear and distinct, and I shall behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face.
Together with the assembly of holy beings, he will hold a lotus pedestal in his hands to welcome and lead me forth; in a single kṣaṇa, [I shall be reborn].
Born before the Buddha, they shall fulfill the bodhisattva path and extensively deliver sentient beings, so that all may together achieve the wisdom of all modes (recite three times;
if time is short or circumstances are urgent, reciting once is also permissible). [Rise and say:]
Having finished the repentance and the making of vows, take refuge and pay homage to Amitābha Buddha and all the Triple Gem (one prostration).

(Next, perform the circumambulation—either three times, seven times, or even many times. While doing so, recite as follows, according to your inclination and the number of circuits, without restriction on the count.)
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Homage to the assembly of pure great ocean-like Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, I vow that all sentient beings shall realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind. (One prostration)
I take refuge in the Dharma. May all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
(One prostration) I take refuge in the Sangha. May all sentient beings preside over the great assembly, free from all hindrances.
(One prostration) Homage to the Noble Assembly.

The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color; His marks and signs and radiance are peerless.
His white tuft curls like five Mount Sumerus; His deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
Within the light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear, And the assembly of transformed Bodhisattvas is likewise boundless.
By means of the forty-eight vows, they deliver sentient beings, Causing those of all nine grades to ascend to the other shore.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, The Greatly Compassionate and Kind One, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.

Namo Amitābha Buddha (Every morning upon rising, recite this a fixed number of times—such as ten thousand, twelve thousand, or even one hundred thousand times—until evening, while facing west and dedicating the merit).

Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean Assembly (This is the Vow Text for Rebirth in the Western Land from Yunqi; the Dedication reads as follows):
I bow my head to the lands of peace and bliss in the four directions, And to the Great Teachers who guide and receive sentient beings.
Now I make this vow, wishing to be reborn there; I pray only that you will compassionately take me in with your grace.

(1. Vow to Hold the Name upon Generating the Mind of Enlightenment) I, disciple [Name], for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the dharma realm, seek the path of the Buddhas' supreme enlightenment of the One Vehicle;
therefore, with single-minded devotion, I shall hold and recite the vast and majestic name of Amitābha Buddha, vowing to be born in the Pure Land.

(3. Vow of Repentance for the Three Obstructions) Furthermore, because my karma is heavy and my merit is slight, my obstructions are deep and my wisdom shallow; my defiled mind is easily inflamed, while pure virtue is difficult to accomplish.
Now, before the Buddha, with my five limbs uplifted in diligence, I bare my heart with single-minded devotion and offer a sincere confession.

For myself and all sentient beings, from beginningless kalpas until now, we have been deluded regarding our inherently pure mind; we have indulged in greed, anger, and ignorance, defiling the three karmas.

The immeasurable and boundless sins and impurities we have committed, and the immeasurable and boundless karmic retributions of enmity we have forged—I pray that they may all be completely extinguished. (The section on establishing the Four Great Vows, part three) From this day forward...
I establish profound vows: to remain far removed from unwholesome dharmas and vow never again to commit them; to diligently cultivate the Noble Path and vow never to fall back or become indolent;
and to vow to attain Perfect Enlightenment and vow to deliver all sentient beings. (First, the vow to invoke the Buddha’s protective mindfulness:

Amitābha Buddha, by the power of your compassionate vows, please bear witness to me, have pity on me, and bestow your grace upon me. May I, within my meditative contemplation and even during my dreams, behold [the Buddha].
Amitābha Buddha! With this present physical body, may I traverse the land of Amitābha Buddha’s Jewel Adornment;
may I receive the consecration of nectar from Amitābha Buddha; may his radiance illuminate my body, his hand stroke my head, and his robe cover my frame.
(2) The Vow for Attaining Auspicious Responses: May my past karmic obstructions be naturally eliminated and my roots of goodness increase;

may afflictions be swiftly emptied and ignorance suddenly shattered, so that the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment may open up in vast clarity, and the true realm of quiescent light may be constantly manifest before me. (3) The Vow for Valuing the Moment of Death: When I am about to reach the end of my life...
Knowing in advance that the time had arrived, his body was free from all illness, suffering, and calamities; his mind was free from all attachment and delusion.
His faculties were joyful and serene, his right mindfulness was clear and distinct, and he cast off his life-retribution with composure, as if entering meditative concentration. Amitābha Buddha.
Together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of all noble sages, they emit light to welcome and guide me, lowering their hands to take me by the hand.

With its multi-storied pavilions, banners, pennants, exquisite fragrances, and celestial music, the sacred realm of the West is revealed before my eyes, causing all sentient beings who see or hear it to rejoice, feel moved, and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
(The Fourth Vow: Seeking Rebirth in the Pure Land) At that time, I shall mount a platform of golden light and follow the Buddha.

Thereafter, in the space of a finger-snap, they will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within a pool of the seven treasures, amidst a supreme lotus flower, the flower shall open and they shall behold the Buddha.

They shall see all the bodhisattvas and hear the wondrous sound of the Dharma, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). In an instant, they shall serve the various Buddhas and personally receive their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Having received this prediction, they shall [attain] the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, and immeasurable hundreds...
Having fully accomplished all merits through the thousand *dhāraṇī* gates, he then returns to the Sahā world from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) without fail.
Dividing his body into countless forms, he pervades the lands of the ten directions, employing inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers.

Through various skillful means, I shall deliver sentient beings, causing them all to leave defilement behind and regain their pure minds, so that they may together be born in the Western Land and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
Although the world is thus inexhaustible, and sentient beings, karma, and afflictions are all inexhaustible, my vow shall be inexhaustible.
(Sixth: General Dedication of Merit) May the merit now generated from prostrating to the Buddha, making vows, and practicing cultivation be dedicated for the benefit of all.

May all sentient beings repay the four debts of gratitude and provide sustenance for those in the three realms of existence. May all beings throughout the Dharma-realm together realize the wisdom of all-encompassing enlightenment.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

A Poem on Bowing to the Holy Assembly and Prohibiting Killing while Releasing Captured Creatures (with Preface) It is heard that for those who protect living beings,
the foremost principles are abstaining from killing and being fond of giving. For those who accumulate merit, the primary means are releasing captured creatures and ransoming lives.
Life comes first. Observe the various classes of beings—those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, and those that fly or crawl;
none are not like me, for we all share one and the same body. How can one rely on strength to oppress the weak?
Yet all who possess blood and breath crave life and dread death; thus, when they encounter capture, they flee, even though their bodies cannot escape and their lives cannot be saved.
Yet, to behold its quivering form and hear its piteous cries is truly most tragic.
Thus, the ancients said: "Seeing them alive, one cannot bear to see them die; hearing their cries, one cannot bear to eat their flesh."

With repeated and earnest exhortations, these words have been made clear to their ears and eyes. I urge all people of the world to refrain from killing and release living beings, and instead observe the fast and recite the Buddha’s name.
In this present life, they will surely tread the path of benevolence and longevity; in future lives, they shall together enter the Land of Lotus Flowers.
Then my wish will perhaps find some consolation.

Your benevolent influence has reached me, yet our conversation is still too brief. To examine the past and verify the present, you already understand this. Do not say there is no karmic retribution for releasing living beings;
at the moment of execution, one does not fail the Master Shou.

The lingering influence of the flowing waters endures for ten thousand ages. The spring provides sustenance for the movement of the cosmos, bringing life to the fish. It relieves hunger, preaches the Dharma, and receives excellent seeds;
observe now the moment when devas and humans receive their prophecies.

His sincerity moved the people so that his divinations were never in vain; he followed the *Laozi* and the *Yijing*, offering sacrifices to pray for sweet rain. The compassionate influence of Emperor Wu of Liang has not yet vanished;
he who temporarily presided over the Way spread it throughout the southeast.

Scales, shells, feathers, and fur cannot be mistaken; though their forms are dull and diverse, their nature is no different. How much of the residual retribution from past lives remains across antiquity and today?
It is not only the Marquis of Sui who obtained the precious pearl.

Do not recklessly cook the arrayed dishes of the kitchen; you must know that all possess life and recognize the sentiment of benevolence. Since Master Pan departed, the rivers and lakes have been in turmoil;
the aquatic creatures wail in sorrow, finding no peace.
Originally wishing to escape this life, on what could one rely? The monkey hangs with sorrowful tears as my soul soars in dreams. I now earnestly exhort you gentlemen:
you should emulate the King of Shang who untied the nets and enclosures.
Ji Sheng harbors a single heart of benevolence; he may easily change his humble name to be selected as a leader. What is even more strange is the seal and toggle of the "Benevolent" (*ren*) title;
all that has been conferred is merely a reliance upon his benevolence.
Mao Bao rescued his soldiers when he was defeated in battle; Ying Zhen’s longevity was likewise clearly increased. A turtle knew to repay its debt on the day its mistress was in peril;
liberation, it turns out, relies upon the practice of releasing living beings.
In those days, he was not merely a young novice; there was also the village elder Yuan who humbled himself before the Master. When his life span ended, he returned with added years of longevity;
the efficacy of his benevolence surpassed that of ingesting divine mushrooms.

Truly following and conforming to the Supreme Deity’s heart that loves life, the Sage’s words have not permitted the use of blade or block. Having long accumulated the merit of compassion, the dragons and heavens rejoice;
longevity shall naturally extend and blessings shall naturally arrive.

The sword-sheath is deeply hidden—this is what I contemplate. Originally, Heaven bestowed benevolence and compassion upon the world. I wish for the mountains and forests to be transformed into King Wen’s park;
may the unified peace and tranquility delight in this flourishing era.

The celestial realms welcome him from afar without false pretense; he still cherishes the memory of his former life as the Buddha who saved the dove. He recalls how the severed bow led to his entry into the ranks of the immortals;
thus the three teachings ultimately converge into a single essence of benevolence.
Whenever one encounters living beings, one should immediately resolve upon the Three Refuges.

(Now, while the precept against killing and the practice of releasing life serve to sustain one's worldly body and life, there is now a means for transcending the world that may likewise be practiced. Whenever we encounter any living being anywhere, we must necessarily give rise to the bodhicitta and cultivate thoughts of compassion.
Taking pity on their ignorance of the Holy Dharma, we shall act as their representatives to take refuge, repent, and make vows, reciting as follows:)
All evil karma created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced by body, speech, and mind— I now seek repentance for all beings.
Sentient beings are infinite; I vow to deliver them all. Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all.
I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma gates; I vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
I vow to deliver all sentient beings of self-nature; I vow to sever the afflictions of self-nature;
I vow to study the Dharma gates of self-nature; I vow to realize the Buddha-way of self-nature.
I, the disciple [Name], on behalf of all sentient beings, take refuge, repent, and make this vow.

By this merit, may all sentient beings universally aspire to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, where they may behold Amitābha. Thereafter, may they manifest emanations to extensively deliver all living beings, so that all together attain the Way of the Buddha.

(Receiving these benefits of the Dharma, one continues the life-force of wisdom in others; this may be called eternally establishing the seeds of the Path. Although this Dharma-gate is said to be a skillful means, the karmic conditions it establishes for the Dharma are exceedingly easy to expand. May the four debts of gratitude be fully repaid and the three realms of existence equally sustained, so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may together perfect the All-Knowing Wisdom.)
